review:
A fantastic game.  I enjoyed everything from the gameplay, aesthetics, to the combat and even the story.  It's very well put together and a big step in the right direction for Deck 13 Interactive (who also made Lords of the Fallen). It's one of those few games that sticks with you....or at least it did with me, and therefore I highly recommend it.

You should pick up this game if....
 - you like Dark Souls (or souls-like) games
 - you like a BIG challenges and learning from your mistakes and can learn to be patient!
 - you like single player.... no multi player ;(
 - you do not want your hand held. you learn as you go!! you don't get anything spoon fed to you except for the very basics
 - you like dystopian futuristic settings
 - you like cutting off limbs in brutal fashion, and using said limbs to craft gear for your awesome character
 - you don't have hundreds of hours to play videogames (the game is relatively short, but that's a good thing in my book)

You may not like this game if.....
 - you are all about story  (i personally like the story, but its one of those things you have to go searching for...and even then it doesn't make the most sense) It's ok, not the best.
 - you are looking for a 'chill' game. You HAVE to pay attention in this game or you will Die....A LOT.
 - you are looking for multiplayer or PVP.....none here
 - you hate dark souls or souls-like games

I hope this has been helpfull.

This game is like Dark Souls with some awesome sci-fi setting and lots of eye candy.

What does that mean?

Dark Souls formula has a couple of specific rules:

1.  EVERY enemy in the game can kill you in seconds.  Even the easiest peon can get you if you aren't paying attention.  As you progress and gain power, these enemies get faster and easier to kill but nothing is ever safe in this game.

2. When you kill stuff and collect XP/Souls/Tech you carry them on your person.  If you die, they are lying on the floor where you were killed.  This means you need to fight your way back to your body to get that XP back.  The Surge has an additional twist, giving you an XP "bonus" for the more you are holding on your person - a risk/reward system for those daring enough to try it.

When you combine parts 1 and 2 you can reach the "difficult" part of this game.  Say you get pretty far into a new area and there is a really tough enemy that jumps out and kills you - then you get back to that spot only to die a 2nd time.  Now you start to get flustered and start skipping enemies and just trying to get back for that XP cache because it's 3 levels worth at this point, then some dumb monster you've killed 50 times takes a swipe at you and another one jumps and you are dead.  3 levels gone and your controller is through the window.

The levels themselves are long and elaborate, with lots of branching paths, locked doors, and secret passages.  These are used as shortcuts to some areas of the level.  Typically you will have a "hub" you start in, and you have to make your way though a section until you've unlocked the door/elevator/power grid that enables a shortcut back to base.  From then on, you can start at this shortcut and move on making progress through the level unlocking more of these until you've reached the end boss and finished the area.

Combat uses a lock-on mechanism with lots of swipes, feints, jumping in and out.  Each enemy has it's own behaviors and one of the tricks of this game is learning how to deal with each type effectively with your chosen weapon.  The weapons themselves all have their own flavor of damage, stun, speed and combos and it's worth trying out the various types until you find the one you like.  I settled on the single-rigged style of weapons for my first playthrough and enjoy them immensely.  One thing I like here is that EVERY weapon is viable and can be used to the end of the game.  The first boss drops a nice weapon that I used for about 90% of my playthrough.

The game is VERY pretty.  Lots of glowing, sparking weapons, condiuts.  There is distortion from gas and various weapons.  The metaliic surfaces all reflect the light and just look gorgeous.  If you have played any of the Dark Souls and are tired of the various shades of brown and death this is a refreshing look for the genre.

I've just finished my 1st playthrough at about 45 hours and I feel there is a lot of value here.  I have not purchased the DLC but I'm thinking about it.  I haven't decided yet whether to jump right into new game+ or to give it a break and come back.

Overall this was a great surprise when I found it and I'm very pleased I did.

Too bad, Steam does only have recommend or don't recommend. Otherwise this would have gotten my 'recommended to some' approval.

What can I say about the surge so far? I like it. I'll be making some comparisons to both Dark Souls and Lords of the Fallen here (The devlopers previous game)

First off let's talk about what they improved over Lords of the Fallen (The developers first push forward in to souls-lke territory) they improved pretty much everything over the community dubbed 'Clunky Souls'. It's no longer clunky that's for sure, combat and just movement in general is smooth and quite fast paced. 

Combat has some interesting mechanics. You can't parry like you can in dark souls and you can't move while blocking like you can in Dark Souls and LoTF. When you block you are stationary BUT they did add in a neat little counter mechanic in the form of ducking and jumping. While blocking you can duck under an enemy attack and then counter or you can jump over the enemy attack and counter that way. It still requires the same sort of timing as say a parry in the DS series. Not being able to move while blocking would usually annoy the hell out of me but with those little added mechanics I can deffinately give it a pass.

Rather than rolling like DS/LoTF you have a Bloodborne style of dodging which again, is a wonderful addition and helps combat feel a lot faster (You'll be using this dodging a lot) You can combine these dodges with attacks too that create good combat openers that effectively stagger your enemy, allowing you to get a good couple of hits off before you back away.

Combat is smooth, it's fluid and such a HUGE improvement over their previous entry. It's also pretty damn difficult too. Unlike LoTF, the enemies in 'The Surge' do not screw around and will severely punish you if you make a mistake (This isn't a negative, this is exactly what us souls-like fans want) and that's just the regular enemies, the bosses are tough as nails. In LoTF 90% of the bosses were a joke to be honest but in 'The Surge' the two bosses I have fought so far have given me some real challenge.

For somebody like me who has put a ridiculous amount of hours in to the soulsborne series it's easy to get to grips with the mechanics, you go in to a boss fight knowing what you should look for, what you should pay attention to and such since you're so used to fighting bosses in a souls-like game but even then for me it was still a challenge, I imagine for those not used to souls-like games it would be an even bigger challenge.

The way gear is handled in this game in my opinion is a HUGE improvement over not only LoTF but the souls games as well (Yes that's right, I said it) In the Souls games you can kill up to 50 maybe a little less of the same enemy and cross every part of your body to just -hope- you get an armour or weapon drop, it becomes tedious and crushes your soul (No pun intended)

In The Surge however with the way you can target enemy limbs you are 100% promised at the very least a schamtic to craft that portion of armour and once you have that schematic you can cut off that same limb of the same enemy in order to get the componants to craft/upgrade said piece. Now it is not lost on me how grindy that feels and I don't really like grinding but it is still less of a grind that farming armour/weapon drops in the souls series. It's not based off pure luck in The Surge and you -always- know what you have to work toward.

So how about the world design? It stacks up to the souls series of games in layout but not in design. It's all inter-conected, full of shortcuts to unlock, secrets to find, hidden weapons and implants to find etc.. like you'd expect of any souls-like game but the world doesn't tell a story in design the way that the souls games do. To their credit they gave it one hell of a try and while the world and story elements, NPC that you meet etc.. are quite interesting, it doesn't grip me the way Lordran/Drangleic/Lothric did.

That's not really a bad thing, those are hard world designs to beat.

People have been calling this game a "Cheap Dark Souls" or a "Ripoff" or a "Cash in" but it's really none of those. It takes the souls formula but then does enough of its own thing to make it stand out from the rest in new and interesting ways which is what game design is all about really, improving ideas and concepts for others to then improve in the future and improve our quality of entertainment overall.

This game also runs flawlessly. I have yet to encounter any graphical glitches, any FPS slowdowns or any crashes. It's a very stable game on my system at least.

Now that the praise is out of the way however, I will talk about the issues the game does seem to have. Firstly it does have a few bugs such as not being able to talk to NPC's which will require you to restart the game, not being able to pick up items which again, requires a restart of the game and also buggy enemy AI that sometimes (Although rarely) notices you WAY before the point they should notice you, we're talking through walls and up stairwells here, that's not acceptable.

There was a certain point where I was fighting an enemy at the top of a stairwell, killed him, started walking down the stairwell only to be greeted by five enemies at the bottom all trying to get up the stairs (We're talking a stairwell that goes down six levels here) so I manage to pull agro from five enemies while being six levels above them, that's not acceptable ever.

One other downer is the lack of a fast travel system. Now usually I don't require fast travel, more often than not in my souls runs I will not bother with fast travel but this game severely  needs it. It's really difficult to find your way to past areas, often you have to jump through a shit load of hoops and if you want to get to a specific area you'll find yourself having to manually travel to and through the previous areas in order to get to where you actually want to be and then when you're done? You have to go back through all the areas you just came. It's very tedious and one of the worst flaws the game has.

All in all though I'd give the game a solid thumbs up. I'm really enjoying it so far and I can see myself enjoying it for a while to come yet. Highly reccomend you pick this up whether you're a fan of souls-like games or just a fan of action/RPG type games in general.

I completed this game on the Xbox a loooong time ago, and seeing the Mixed reviews on Steam, I could only assumed the game was poorly ported to PC. Now I'm replaying it... nope! I honestly don't get the hate, I suspect this may just come down to folks expecting more Souls-aligned gameplay/design, and not getting it. 

Brief summary, this is in the action-rpg field, and does contain many of the trappings of Soulslike games. Fairly challenging gameplay (I'd say this leans a little easier than many in this genre), big boss fights that, once cleared, are largely gone for good, save points where you can assign points you've accrued from killing mobs to level up stats. All that good stuff. 

Where this one differs is the combat is limb-based, which is to say you fight an enemy and you choose something to focus on. This is actually a really fun mix on the formula, as it allows you not just to adapt to certain enemies and their weaknesses, but also you perform finishers if you're performing well and... well, no easy way to say this, steal said limb. So if you see an enemy with a giant hammer and you think "gosh I sure would like to have that hammer..." then there's a pretty solid chance you're able to get and use said hammer. And as you kill and scrap enemies, if you collect bits you already have, they're converted into upgrade materials for those same items. It's a unique gimmick, offers up some fun combat variation, plenty armour/weaponry to collect. All in all, I really enjoy this aspect of the game.

Story wise, nothing to write home about. Intro movie is dope, early story beats of where you are, why things are as they are? Intriguing enough to keep you playing. Wouldn't say the pay-off is anything huge. But few people play games like this for the story, and I dare a single one of you out there to pretend any Dark Souls game has award winning narratives.

So, I don't get the hate on this, truly. Lots of stuff to collect, a fun way to collect it, big levels with varied design. If you like the soulslike genre but are open to variations on the theme, this is for you. If you're a hyper-purist who demands bonfires and individual stat leveling, maybe not.

I should probably point out that, despite my eventual dismay about this game, I actually enjoyed the first 5-10 hours of The Surge. However, in the end, the game delivers merely an idea, and fails to live up to most of the sums of its parts.

The idea within the combat system of targetting body parts, and your moveset being different depending on what you are targetting is pretty cool. It was very well realized in the first two levels with the normal enemies. However, as the game goes on you begin to realize barely any of the combos and attack tactics will ever work. Most enemies later on can only be taken on with cheesy methods of dash stabbing, slide tackling, and general hit and run tedium. There is no robust parry and evasion (you can dash, but i-frames are terrible, and blocking is so clunky and unresponsive, with a terrible add-on of having a jump and duck mechanic which is borderline impossible to utilize) system, especially on the enemy's part. Instead, the developers just load them up with adamantine poise levels, and the magic ability to hit way faster than you ever can, with the force of Thor's hammer, staggering you to kingdom come. Later on you get enemies firing flamethrowers and grenades, while you hopelessly try to close the gap with your melee weapons, and they insta kick you down chunking half your health... bleh.

Character progression is so horrible it's soul destroying. Upgrading is tragically linear and gated, there aren't enough weapons, and even if there were, there is a terrible weapon proficiency mechanic (presumably added when the devs realized there would be no motivation to actually kill mobs anymore i.e: the only part of the game worth a damn) that more or less limits you to one weapon type.

Level design I found very interesting with the shortcut unlocking, but the design is so uniform and indistinctive that from the second level onward you will have no notion of where you are going, and out of frustration will probably miss areas. There really should have been a metroidvania style map here. 

All in all, there is just no drive for the player to keep coming back once he or she hits the brick wall of tedium. The combat system needs reworking, and I just wish Deck 13 would hire someone to make a more robust and responsive sense of melee combat that works within some semblence of balance. Even if you could find your way to enjoying the stilted rules of combat here, there is nothing else driving you forward other than just plodding your way through the environment to get to the end of the game.

The Surge is a really good idea on paper, with a pretty tragic implementation.

This is an absolutely outstanding game and after reading a lot of the reviews it seems that the negative reviews are based more around peoples inability rather than the game itself. So I will go into more detail if possible by giveing each section a score out of 10.


PROS!

-Performence

It is astonishingly good. I am runningt he game at over 100fps 1440p constantly with no drops below at all. This is on the highest possible settings and on an average computer (i5 and a 980ti). 9/10

-Graphics 

They are beautiful. The world is fantastic to look at, and the characters are very well detailed. There are a few low res textures here and there but they tend to be off the beaten path so do not cause any isses. Enemies are detailed and have a nice amount of variety in looks. 9/10

-Armor

The exo suits are awesome. There is a huge variet in them and all of them have lots of detail. They also provide set bonus' which does help but if you want to mix and match you are more than able to with not much of a drawback. 8/10

-Weapons

There are several types of weapons and they all feel and perform differently, but all weapons within that catagory tend to be the same with some changes but I will get into that later. They look brilliant though, all of them look like the killing machines they are meant to be and have nice effects etc. 6/10

-Combat

Here is the big one for most people. I personally love it, if you learn how to use it you will be a monster in no time. There is a learning curve to it that will punnish spammers and people that do not pay attention to stats and enemies abilities. The 'Impact' stat is pretty self explanatory. The more you have the more you stagger so the more hits you can get in and the more damage you can do. Or in the case of weapons with low impact you can get lots of fast hits in and then move away.

It is pretty standard RPG stuff to be honest. On a side note if you got on with the Lord of the Fallen combat (like me) you will fall right into your groove with this game and not have many issues at all. Overall I would say the combat is absolutely flawless, if you learn how the game plays and what abilites to use in the situation you will get on with it very well. It rewards people that think about that sort of thing instead of spamming away. 10/10.

-Leveling

You level up in the same way as most games of this genre by collecting 'souls' or in this case scrap. You take that to a medbay where you can invest it into your suits core to increase its power. The result is a higher core level, this allows you to equip 'Implants' these are things like more HP/Stamina/Energy and your healing items and so on. Also your armor pieces have energy requirements so the better the armor the more you will need. This actually works incredibly well, especially with the ability to bank your scrap so you can acess it later. 8/10

-Looting Mechanic

I am a huge fan of this. Enemies have 6 spots on them you can manually target. 2 arms 2 legs chest and head. If there is a piece of armor you are after and you see a guy wearing it, beat the snot out of that body part and rip it off him. Theres a weapon you want and you see a guy wielding that badboy? Cut that guys arm off and its yours! You get the schematic for the armor and then you can make it at a workshop. All weapons and armor are upgradeable and each NG cycle you go through their level cap is raised by 5. Its simple enough to work out and execute. 9/10

CONS

I honestly dont think there are any of real note aside from the few I will mention now.

-NG+ onwards

After beating the game you go straight into NG+ and as you probably know the game begins again. All your armor and weapons can be increased by 5 more levels, you have more slots for Implants avilable and you earn more scrap. I personally found NG+, NG++ and NG+++ to be an absolute cakewalk. On my first playthrough I was smashed about constantly and I loved it. But from then on the game was too easy, aside from a few extra enemies everything is in exactly the same spot and behave the exact same way. Yeah they hit harder but at this point you have more HP and damage than they can cope with and you destroy them in 2 hits up until maybe 2/3 of the way through then its 3 shots for the rest of the game. Sadly this suffers with Lords of the Fallen syndrome where after NG+ you may as well start a new character since you get nothing out of it. 4/10

-Content is a little lacking

It is not a long game, my first playthrough where I explored every single nook and cranny took me about 40 hours. after that I did a dew NG+ cycles and added about another 20 hours and at that point I had every item in the game and all the achievements. It left me with a little bit of disapointment that I didnt have more to do. I wanted to keep tearing peoples limbs off because I liked their shiny armor. Hopefully there will be some DLC that adds more but thats not relevant at the moment. 5/10

-Story/Voice acting

I put these together since they ggo hand in hand really. Both are a bit 'meh'. The story is a cool idea has some great cutscenes but it is pretty thin. If you listen to every audio log then you get a better lay of the land but its pretty generic to be honest. The voice acting just adds to this since it feels pretty wooden and rushed, but since there isnt much of it then it isnt the end of the world. The main characters voice actor is pretty good though. 6/10


This game is great, if you ingnore the Dark Souls fanboys that hate the combat because they cant spam with their Carthas Curved swords or poke with their Estocs then you will see that this games combat is a masterpiece. The whole game from start to finish made me smile with the grusome fighting and the incredibly satisfying gameplay. 

If you are looking for 50-60 hours of violence and feeling like a hero then this is the game for you. Overall I would give it a 9/10.

A catastrophic event has knocked you out during the first day on the job… you wake up equipped with a heavy-grade exoskeleton, in a destroyed section of the complex. Robots gone haywire, insane augmented co-workers and rogue AI - everything wants you dead.

[h1] TL:DR at the bottom of this review [/h1]

[h1] Combat [/h1]
Combat feels smooth, unique, and fast paced. You can block attacks, duck under them, or even jump over them. Dodging is also smooth. There are also 5 different types of weapons, from staves to swords to huge hammers and axes. Each type has their own movesets and combos you can make, you can also include dodging and blocks to your combos. There will hopefully be a weapon type that suits your style, you just gotta find it. Each weapon type has weapon proficiency, which is your weapon level. Oh and enemies get harder the more you progress.

[h1] Crafting [/h1]
Crafting is simple and sort of tedious. You need to cut an armored body part to obtain the schematic and then head to the Operations Room (which is basically home base) to craft the armor piece, given you have the materials needed. Each upgrade requires credits and a better material which are in MKs (MK1,MK2,MK3,MK4 etc.). Materials are found by cutting armor pieces you already have the schematic for, instead of another schematic, you get the materials needed to make that armor piece. This may become an annoyance for people.

[h1] Armor [/h1]
Pretty neat. There are 3 types of armor, Operator, Goliath, and Sentinel. Goliath absorbs more damage, Operator consumes less stamina, and Sentinel is in the middle, providing good defense and stamina consumption. Each armor set has their own bonus. Some are great, some are horrible. You can also mix and match armor sets.

[h1] Leveling up and Implants [/h1]
Unique. To level up, you need to increase your core power in the Operations Room. It will cost more credits each time you level up. You need core power to use your armor and implants. Implants are used to help you survive the onslaught of bosses and normal enemies alike. There are many implants, from healing stimulants to damage boosters to even core power extensions. Almost all implants use core power, the more advanced, the more core power it takes to use that implant. You get more implant slots by finding the newer exo suits and the more you level up your core power.

[h1] Audio [/h1]
Not much to say. The boss music is no where close to as good as dark souls and the Operations Room's music can be really annoying, but that's just me. Luckily, someone made a guide on how to change the music to whatever you want! The voice acting is decent, the enemies make audio prompts that sound like they just got hot coffee spilled on them or if they got triggered because someone disagreed with their opinion

[h1] The story [/h1]
I don't even know, I was too busy running away from enemies to even care. Just read the wiki or someone else's review.

[h1] The environment [/h1]
Very good. Really feels like a huge factory and you can get a picture of what it may look like before everyone went nuts. There are 5 major areas.

[h1] Bosses [/h1]
Challenging, and fun, but too few bosses. There are 5 bosses in The Surge and each have their own story and movesets. Each boss drops a weapon and a buttload of credits. [spoiler]If you kill them in a certain way, you can get their special boss weapon. Which is just a V2 of the same weapon if you killed the boss in a normal way [/spoiler]

[h1] Pricing [/h1]
Expensive. Buy it on a sale or on a trusted 3rd party site. Or if you want to be a badass, buy the game in full price. The major dlc, (A Walk in the Park) is quite pricey for what it offers, buy it if you are a badass or a big fan or just wait for a sale too. The CREO Special Employee Kit is not worth it because from what I heard, you just get 2 implants and a color for your exo suit.

[h1] Controls [/h1]
Great. There is controller support and keyboard+mouse support. They both have great bindings and it comes down to what you prefer more. A keyboard and mouse, or a controller?

[h1] Difficulty [/h1]
Challenging. I don't have much to say about the difficulty, but you will either find this game harder than what others say, or easier than what others say. It just comes down to experience and your capability to accept defeat and death.

[h1] TL:DR [/h1]
-Great combat
-Simple, but slightly tedious crafting
-Cool armor system
-Unique leveling-up system
-Unique Implant system
-Good audio
-Don't know about the story
-Amazing environment
-Challenging and fun bosses, but too few
-Buy on sale (including dlcs)
-Nice graphics
-Great controller and keyboard+mouse support
-Challenging and sometimes unforgiving difficulty

Thank you for taking the time to read my review, if you did.

Incredible game, and strangely underrated. I almost didn't buy it because of the reviews, but I'm glad I listened to my instincts (sci-fi Dark Souls? yes please!). I just finished it after 31 hours of play (I play slow and methodically). Combat is insanely fun and rich - I spent hours grinding for tech scrap to level up and had a blast the whole time. 

The game is good in ways it doesn't even need to be - audiologs, NPCs, all with really good voice acting - and the story is appropriately interesting and grim. It also has fantastic level design. There's only one checkpoint per area and as you progress you open up new shortcuts to get back to it.

I really hope this sells enough to warrant a sequel, because this is one of the best games I've played in years. Can't wait to dive into NG+.

In-Depth analysis:

As a old Soulsborne/Nioh/LOTF Veteran i think that might be the hardest in that genre to get into (well, maybe Nioh), but after a while i just realized i just have to adapt myself more. While the gameplay might be the same as other games in that genre, it's still different in a lot of ways, you just have to get into it and forget about everything you learned from the other games. It's nearly pure meele and no way to avoid it, like in other games. You can't just cheese your way trought, use ranged attacks, or overlevel yourself so you have an easier time. You really need to concentrate all the time and be aware what you do. 

When you played said games before you will recognize some mechanics. When you die, you have to get your Tech Scrap (Currency) back and there is a timer to get them back, just like in LOTF. When you die enemies will respawn, same when you are using the Medbay. There are limited options to regain your health at first, but the longer you play the more ways you will find to regain health. Dodging is essential and blocking pretty useless. You have to be mobile and always have an eye on your stamina. When you get greedy you die really fast. 2-3 hits at the beginning are deadly.

Here is where the uniqueness from "The Surge" comes into play. First of all, there is no Skillsystem. Most of your stats will come from your Armor and your Weapon itself. From Stability, Impact, Attack Speed to Defense and Damage. The rest, like Health, Stamina, Energy and everything else comes from all kind of implants you can choose from. So all the Currency you get you will need just for upgrading your "Core Power", so you can use more implants and for crafting and upgrading your gear. 

Setting and Atmosphere is just awesome. You are crawling through dark corridors, always with a claustrophobic feeling, enemies around every corner, nobody knows what's going on and no light at the end of the tunnel. The map outlay can and will be very confusing and it will take a while to get yourself orientated. There are a lot of doors you can't open until later in the game and a every map have a dozen of shortcuts. Overall level design is pretty great. 

While the DLC "A Walk In The Park" is a bit short (around 2 hours) and more on the easier side, it's is totally worth to get. It's adds a fantastic new zone, 2 new bosses, gear sets, weapons, implants and new enemies. Great level design and atmosphere as well. 

The other "real" DLC "The Good, the Bad and the Augmented" adds a series of intersting Test Champers. While the setting is very odd, it is fun for a few hours, but the replay value just isn't there, when you got everything. It is one of the best places to farm Tech Scraps and it contains a few of the strongest implants in the game though.

Long story short, don't compare it to a Soulsborne game too much. While it have the same overall mechanic, it's still quite different. When you like those kind of games, you won't miss out on that hidden gem. It's entertaining, has a unique setting and some great gameplay elements. Just give yourself a chance to get into it and you will love it. I actually liked the game so much i just played trough it twice on my Ps4 and then another two times on Steam, finally getting the full "Augmented Edition" with 100% Archivements. Highly recommended on sale. 

Ps.: Also "The Surge 2" incoming. \o/

I'm writing this review being very close to the end of the game. So far I found it very enjoyable. It's definitely souls-like, although I'm finding it much easier than any game on the Souls series. Dark Souls 1 is probably where the authors took most of their inspiration, seeing as the level design in this game revolves around shortcuts and the combat has a similar feel (with the added fun of dismemberments).

There were some reviews that almost made me not buy this game, so I'm going to address some of the negative points on those:

1) Lack of enemy diversity.
This one is true, but it didn't bother me much. Combat is fun enough and the animations are so detailed it's underestandable why they couldn't create more enemies.

2) Lots of backtracking.
There is some backtracking built into the plot, but it felt natural to me; it's not about having to fetch some mcguffin you left three areas behind and had no way of knowing was neded later. There is also some optional backtracking required if you're a completionist (there are collectibles locked in areas you'll only be able to access after acquiring end game equipment), but it's entirely optional.

3) Lack of a map or proper direction to progress the plot.
I guess people who complained about this aren't fans of Dark Souls. Not only it didn't bother me, but I found the progression in this game almost linear. There are frequent branching paths, but they are mostly shortcuts back to the Med bay and short paths to hidden loot. I can imagine having trouble getting my bearings if I stopped playing for a while, but it shouldn't be much of an issue for someone with an average memory.

4) Regular enemies kill you in one hit.
This one had me worried the most. Some guys wrote that they ended up only using running attacks and then backing of, because enemies were so punishing; it sounded terribly boring. Fortunately I found that this can happen, but it depends mostly on the armor and implants you use: if you use light armor and don't equip a few implants that raise your health, you will get one shotted by most enemies; if you play with heavy armor and equip health impants you'll be able to survive a couple of hits from even the strongest enemies.

Finally, I just want to vent about a particular mechanic, that I think detracts from the overall game experience: weapon proficiency. Weapon proficiency boots your damage with a weapon type, is gained through using that weapon type and doesn't seem to have a cap, so it punishes using different weapon types. It's a damn shame this mechanic exists, because I tried all the different weapon types for an achievement and they were all pretty balanced and fun to use.

P.S.: I played this game with mouse and keyboard and it was fine. Unlike Dark Souls, playing with a controller is not a necessity here.

Takes around 25-30 hours to do a 100% play-through (including the DLCs).


[b][u]Positives[/u][/b]
• Some pretty neat ideas in the game. One of the only souls-inspired games that doesn't just lazily copy the leveling system of Dark Souls. The leveling system in this game is really clever, and surprisingly pretty well balanced.
• When it actually works correctly, the limb-targeting system is a very nice way to make this game's combat unique. You can target parts you need to upgrade the equipment you have, or target parts that you want to take from the enemy to equip yourself.


[b][u]Negatives[/u][/b]
• There is absolutely no logic in how the player is supposed to progress at several points in the game. You will completely explore an entire map, end up either at a dead end or back at the start of the map, and have no idea what to do next. Sometimes doors/paths are inexplicably now open in previous maps and you are just somehow supposed to know that you should go to a random point in the previous map, which you've already explored, in order to progress.
• Despite the amount of dialogue, cutscenes, or available NPCs, the game makes absolutely no attempt to communicate to the player what their current goal is. About half the game is probably spent just wandering around aimlessly in maps that you've already fully explored several times trying to figure out what you're supposed to be doing now.
• You'll often hit switches and have absolutely no idea what they do. The game makes no effort to communicate important information to the player.
• The combat system in this game is completely broken. An attack will miss you by a very large distance and the game will still say you took massive damage from it.
• The combat system is deliberately designed so you can really only take on one enemy at a time, so of course the developers make it "challenging" by constantly surrounding the player with enemies that just relentlessly attack in a group.
• Often times the game will not register that the player has pressed the dodge button, or will dodge in a different direction than the player said to, of course causing the player to then take a lot of damage or even die. Other times it will do the dodge and successfully avoid the attack, but just say that you got hit by it anyways.
• The limb-targeting system is very frustrating to use. I often have to spend more time trying to get the game to lock on to a specific limb than I do actually fighting an enemy. Targeting a specific limb is usually very finicky, and after you finally do get the limb you want the game will often just snap back to another limb because the game doesn't have a dead zone set for the right analog stick.
• Enemies are often very poorly designed, and the bosses feel like very little effort was put into designing their attacks. The developers have no clue how to make an enemy challenging properly. A lot of times they just rely on surrounding the player with enemies or boss fights with a bunch of unavoidable/sporadic attacks. Boss fights often feel like a gear check, making sure you have enough meds to tank all of the unavoidable hits long enough to drain the boss's health bar.
• The game will occasionally stop rendering the visuals of enemy attacks. For example, if an enemy is using a flamethrower it would make the sound of fire being sprayed, but no fire can be seen. Many attacks in this game rely on these types of visual effects so this can be completely game-breaking when it happens.
• The map design in this game is the absolute laziest I have ever seen. Many areas of the map are awkwardly connected by long tunnels. You probably spend around 30% of the game just running through these horribly designed tunnels because the map designers didn't want to find creative ways to connect the maps like From Software does.
• Every map is a labyrinth. The game has way too many shortcut paths going back to the same locations, and it makes navigating the maps an absolute nightmare, particularly so if you take a short break from the game and then come back to it (seriously, good luck figuring out which of the 50 paths out of the medbay area is the one you're supposed to be on - you'll just keep circling back to the medbay over and over and over and over, losing your mind).
• A lot of issues with the camera not being where it should, being difficult to control, or finding a way to jam itself up against an enemy or wall so the player cannot see what they're doing.
• Game randomly crashed several times.
• The game has a lot of issues with the Steam overlay. It's very slow to respond and multiple times it caused my graphics driver to crash (causing my PC to freeze up until the game eventually crashed).
• Playing in fullscreen mode has a lot of issues with alt-tabbing, but playing in borderless windowed mode causes frame rates to be very unstable and the game to lag severely in areas where it would be very smooth in fullscreen mode.
• The story for this game isn't interesting at all.

The team behind Lords of the Fallen have another go at the souls-like genre, and it's a better game fullstop. It's actually more like Bloodborne than Dark Souls as the combat is faster paced with an emphasis on dodging, and trying to tank anything will result in a swift(er) demise. Yes, it's a challenging game, punishing even but never unfair and the progress feels just right. 
Combat is good, with everything feeling meaty. It's also fairly unique that the gear and weapons you get are mainly sourced from cutting them from enemies. Upgrades require more parts, so do you go for that armoured chest on the enemy or the unarmoured head? The formers rewards are higher but comes with greater risk. It's a nice system with plenty of scope for different builds and playstyles.

The futuristic/apocalyptic setting is very well done and the visuals are excellent, with great animations and sharp texturing. The sound is also top notch, and you can even add your own music to the Ops centres, these are your basic hubs throughtout the game where you can upgrade parts and implants and take a breather. I first played The Surge when it released in 2017, I very much had a love/hate relationship with it. Now, two years later, having played through a second time I can say for certain that there is no more hate-- this game is great! 

[h1] Pros [/h1]
[*][u] The combat[/u] is reminiscent of Bloodborne's fast paced action, with, of course, some unique additions. Every weapon class has a whole set of combos to master-- and some special weapons have extra moves for specific combos. Many of these feel fantastic to pull off, and help keep combat from feeling dull despite most enemies being similar. Instead of waiting for enemies' one percent drop chance armor to fall-- you can go right for whatever you want. Like their helmet? Aim and chop. They have a cool looking hammer? Break their arm and slice it off to take it for yourself. Drones add some utility, ranging from things like reducing all damage taken for a small amount of time, to shooting enemies from far away.
[*][u] The world[/u], despite criticism, wonderfully sets the game's tone. The industrial locales aren't full of dull grays and pure concrete, no-- they're all colorful. Each area is accented by a color theme. The biolabs are full of greens, R&D has reds, service tunnels are orange, lights and signs everywhere pepper in other colors-- this is a singular facility, and it feels like it. All roads lead to Central Production B, you'll constantly find yourself winding back here from a new angle, uncovering more as you progress through the game-- aiding more in creating the feeling of a cohesive world.
[*][u] World building[/u] from characters you meet along your journey, to audiologs you pop into your onboard ipods-- everything helps build up an entertaining world you'll get sucked into-- wanting to learn more. 
[*][u] Implants[/u] allow for a variety of builds while also allowing you to switch up your playstyle whenever you want. Scared of dying? Just equip only healing items, nothing's stopping you! Confident? Play a glass cannon; use damage boosting injections, stamina boosts, energy gains, and drone damage increases-- whatever your playstyle you're likely to be able to find something for you.
[/list]

[h1] Cons [/h1]
[*][u]This game is unfair[/u] at times-- sometimes you'll be pitted against an enemy while you're standing on a two yard wide pathway with no guard rails to prevent you from dodging to your doom. Some areas are a bit too dark-- despite your rig's built in flashlight which is only as effective as a phone screen and you'll find yourself walking into danger. An enemy with a OHKO combo may be placed behind a corner that you can't peak behind, only to discover them by the time you round it with your face firmly plastered into the floor. There are particularly difficult late game enemies which constantly heal themselves, while also packing enough of a punch to OHKO. Luckily you can just run by most of them.
[*][u] The free DLC enemies[/u] that were added between the first time I played and now are a bit very difficult to fight. The new gear they came with are all welcome, for sure-- but these enemies are equipped with thorough knowledge of the game's combos and pack a wallop. That's not a problem on its own, however-- several of these enemies are placed directly along the game's required pathways-- including some early game ones. This makes the game effectively more difficult than it was at launch. I killed each of them, sure, but I did not much enjoy my encounters with them.
[/list]

Despite the game's flaws, I still had a good time playing it. I'd recommend it to anyone with cravings for games similar to Bloodborne or looking for a fun dark sci-fi action game.

So... this is a tough review to formulate. The game is well made, looks good, runs good, the lore is good, the new mechanics are interesting, everything works... however... I didn't find it fun at all.
TLDR: The easiest way I have to describe how this game made me feel is... Imagine Dark Souls, but if the combat didn't feel good and instead of rolling you only had backstepping.

The combat feels... off. I can't quite put my finger on what, but it just lacks either feedback or weight, the weapons just feel like jello. The big weapons are extremely slow. The mid-size weapons feel like crap. The 1 handed swords are the ones that felt the best, but they still lack in feedback. The dodging might be the worst thing of them all tho... You get basically no invincibility frames during it, you are supposed to actually dodge out of the way of an attack instead of rolling "under" it like on Dark Souls. That's a big blow to the game imo, the most fun boss battles in the DS franchise involve lots of dangerous rolling. Also enemies in this game are harder to stagger, kinda of unreliable to know when you are stunning an enemy with your attacks or not. Very often you'll be mashing the attack button in a combo and the enemy will hit you because it didn't stay stunned for long and you didn't notice... again, not a lot of feedback.

The game is pretty hard... as soon as you get to the first boss, you'll know the kid gloves are off. Tho while I won't often detract from a game for being hard, I love very hard games, this game's difficulty is often based on annoying you or being unfair. You'll often question yourself "what am I doing wrong here? Am I missing something? Am I supposed to be doing something else?". The game also loves throwing "traps" at the player... very blatant ones too. Enemies will be hidden around corners and ready to jump at you as soon as your toes are in their line of sight... Dark sous did that too at times, but this game does it literally every 2 or 3 rooms. I'm convinced there's more "sneak attack enemy trap" in one level of this game than there are in the entirety of any Souls game. It gets old fast.

It being hard isn't really the issue here, Dark Souls 3 is extremely hard too, but when combined with the combat issues I explained above... it just isn't fun. Dark Souls is hard, it infuriates and inflicts pain on you... but it's gameplay is also perfect, playing it feels like pure joy, you WANT to master it because the controls, the weapons, the movement, it's all just heaven. On The Surge, however, it's about the same difficulty as the worst parts of the Souls games, the movement feels unresponsive, the weapons feel like crap, dodging is unreliable and doing combos is as rewarding as spreading butter on a slice of bread.  So yea, while just yesterday I beat the 2 hardest DLC bosses in Dark Souls 2 on my own, I ended up quitting about halfway through The Surge... The Fun-to-Frustration ratio wasn't balanced, so I had no desire to continue. It really sucks, I REALLY don't like giving up on a game like this, but at the end of the day, if you aren't having fun with a game, you are wasting your time.

Seeing as this is on sale, it's an appropriate time to post a review for this game. Very simply, I really, really enjoy this game. Yes, it's a Soulsborn-style game (and I'll be comparing it to other games like it as appropriate), but with the "fresh twist" of modern technology. It sets out to do what it wants to, and it does a solid job of it. Is it perfect? No, but that's okay. Here's a very lengthy explanation why. TLDR is at the bottom.

[b] The Story [/b]

Sadly, there isn't too much to write about here. You can avoid most of the overall story in the game and just kinda blunder through enemies and bosses. However, if you look into it, and pay attention to the cutscenes, dialog, and character interactions, it's actually pretty interesting to follow. It kind of falls into the average "tragic hero" trope in the beginning, but there's a fair bit more under the hood that the player can explore if they choose. Personally, I thought the story was particularly interesting and complemented what the game had to offer. It isn't something you're spoon-fed though, and it's not as intriguing as other Soulsborn games where you might pause the game for a bit to go look up the lore. But it's there, and it should be given credit where credit is due.

[b] The Gameplay  [/b]

You've got your stamina bar, you've got your dodge, you've got your whack button, you've got your harder whack button, and you've got your lock on. It's pretty simple to pick up and learn this game, and that's not a bad thing. Anyone who has played a game like this will be able to pick it up relatively easily. I would even go so far as to say this game is easier to pick up then other Soulsborn games, as something about the combat feels a bit easier to get used to. Early on, the enemies aren't nearly as punishing, meaning that you can really get a feel for wind-ups, learn telegraphed moves, and find a playstyle that suits you. Sure, if you're looking for the "punch me in the nether regions as soon as I start" style of game, it might not fit that, but it actually feels like a good entry point into this style of combat. As someone who isn't [i]particularly[/i] good at Soulsborn combat, it was actually really pleasant to "learn" this game, really. That said, it doesn't just "hold your hand" throughout the later encounters, as you'll still have to work for your boss kills and such (unless you're like, a no-damage Souls runner, in which case, why are you reading my review anyways).

[b] The Music [/b]

Now normally this is a point I'd ignore, as I'm usually the type to just put on some background music that doesn't drown out audio queues and play blissfully through the game. But oddly enough, this one struck home. All of the music in the game is [i]decent[/i]. But there's a particularly atmospheric song in the OST, which plays in every medbay in the game (unless you turn it off, which props to the devs for considering that for those who might not want to hear it too much). There's something oddly haunting about the melody, and it feels at home in this game. The song is Prisoner by Stumfol. There's a beautiful melancholy to hearing this melody every time you revive, and it feels like it has two meanings to you: the medbay is a sanctuary and you are safe here, and that you feel alone in this world and need to trudge along to sort out what happened. Very simply, that's a beautiful atmospheric touch to add to the game, and I even found myself smiling as I revived and heard the song. 

The rest of the soundtrack is enjoyable to listen to and adheres to the theme well. Oftentimes you'll be too caught up in the heat of the battle to really give it a listen, but I encourage you to give it a listen sometime.

[b] The Content [/b]

If there's anything you can fault The Surge for, it's for not having too much content. You don't have too many zones, there's a limited roster of bosses, and it's not nearly as open-world as other Soulsborn games. It's not meant to be your "put in hundreds of hours" kind of game. That said, it introduces new concepts to make the most out of what it can. Hard-mode kills on bosses are something to work for and be proud of (and have the show-off potential through weapons), and smelter kills are progressive towards bragging-rights-worthy content. The "hack off what you want" style of gameplay is super cool, in my opinion, and really allows the player to farm or ignore enemies when necessary to suit their playstyle. See an enemy with a piece of armor you like? Target that limb and hack it off of them. Congratulations, you most likely just got a new schematic to make that piece of armor you wanted! To me, this was a really cool feature to have, and I enjoyed it greatly. This mechanic is a lot of the draw that The Surge has, and though ultimately there aren't TOO many weapons and armor sets, it's a really cool mechanic and I enjoyed it a lot.

[b] The Theme [/b]

Alright. Take your favorite Soulsborn, be it DS 1-3, Bloodborn, S&S, what have you. Now, throw it far into the future. Suddenly it's post-apocalyptic and driven by technology. Does that sound appealing? If it does, then this game is definitely for you. If it doesn't, then that's okay, I'm just being honest here. The apocalyptic machine-ridden style isn't for everyone, and I feel like that could be a deal-breaker here if you're adamant about your fantasy style, so it's necessary to state. Personally, I enjoy this theme greatly, and The Surge does it well. The environments are detailed and beautiful, and the wreckage lying around is a good look for the game which adds to the initial feelings of being left alone in a world you don't fully understand. It's a simple theme, but The Surge does a good job with it. 

[b] The Verdict [/b]

If a Soulsborn game beset with rampant machines and literal hack-and-slash gameplay sounds fun to you, I highly recommend you pick up this game. It flew under the radar in a lot of aspects because it didn't do anything perfectly, but it did a lot of things well. The new things that it brought to the table were done well, so if you can get past a smaller-length game, you're sure to have fun with it. It's a solid pick-up to satisfy your Soulsborn craving.

TL;DR: It doesn't revolutionize Soulsborn games, but it does a good job at innovating where it can. It's a bit short, but still worth the time. 

Thanks!
-Scrumpy

This game is goddamned excellent. Bosses are thrilling, but there are only five of them. Combat is tense and exciting throughout. Grinding, leveling and building are ingenious. And the story hit me with two themes surprisingly effectively.

[h1]The Bosses[/h1]

There are only 5 bosses in this game. However, this game makes the absolute most of those 5 encounters. The first boss is your warm-up. It's your introduction to the game. It punishes you if you're bad, though. So, as a beginner, it feels good when you defeat it.

The next four bosses are absolute monsters. Every one of them is O&S or Nameless-King difficult, and each for its own unique reason. Their movesets are very complex, so it's hard to learn their patterns quickly. They also have varied abilities to trap you, meaning they have a move or two that, if they start up while you're in the wrong position, you're toast. And they hit like trucks. Very, very fun boss fights in this game.

[h1]Combat[/h1]

First things first: this game is goddamned hard. By now, in this sort of game, we're used to "trash mobs." These are groups of enemies that merely stand between you and a boss. They're usually dumb and easy unless you lose your patience and do something stupid. However, even a normal enemy standing by himself is a challenge in The Surge. This means there's no such thing as a trash mob. There are mobs from which you try desperately to pull one enemy at a time. Just looking at certain mob makeups will make you shit your pants with fear and rage.

Anyway.

You're a man wearing an exosuit with ability-altering armor welded to it. When you fight, you feel like a man wearing an exosuit with ability-altering armor welded to it. Attacks are really heavy and slow if you're using heavy weapons. They're really bursty and light if you're using the quick weapons.

Defense is suitably complicated. Your dodge is god-tier, no matter your build. You leap whole meters to either side, front or back, and i-frames protect you on your way. If you time your dodge correctly, time will slow down for just a bit. If you attack during the slowdown, you get bonus damage. That's as tasty as it sounds.

You can block, as well. Initiating the block drains a chunk of stamina, then holding the block continuously drains the rest. So, you can't abuse it. If you block at just the right time, then you've parried. Follow it up with attacks for the good damage.

This game has an addition to defense that will give Souls veterans challenge, as well. While blocking, you can press up or down on the right analog stick to either jump or duck for a second. Jump over low attacks, duck under high attacks. Attacking afterward stuns the enemy and amplifies the damage of your next attack. If you're really good, you can use these techniques to burn through enemies really quickly.

Later, you get a drone for ranged attacks. These ranged attacks consume energy, which you build during a fight.

Energy also lets you use injectables (like a special healing item) and execute enemies.

Speaking of executing enemies, let's talk about grinding/leveling/building.

[h1]Grinding/Leveling/Building[/h1]

To me, this is a slog in most games. Build a strength character by committing point after point to the strength attribute. Regret your strength build? Look for a respec item, find the respec NPC, and respec.

The Surge makes me love it. Its method is ingenious.

The four components of grinding/leveling/building are gear, proficiency, implants and power core level.

Gear is obvious--it's what you wear. Each piece of a set has its own perks (defense, stability, stam reduction/increase, damage reduction/increase, etc.). When you're wearing every piece in a set, you get a full-set bonus. One set's bonus, for example, is the Chloranthy ring--stamina regens much, much faster. Another gives you health regen. Yet another grants you lots of bonus damage when you're at full energy. This is the most basic way to determine your character's build.

You get gear by executing enemies in the right way. While fighting, you can target specific body parts with your strikes--head, arm, leg, torso. If you focus your attacks on one before you execute, the execution will tear the body part away from the body. When that happens, the gear held or worn by that body part falls to the ground, and you can pick it up. You obtain weapons straight away. You get armor blueprints, which you use to craft the piece of armor back at the med bay. You also get upgrade materials from the part you chop, which can be used to craft and upgrade armor of the type collected or weapons.

Proficiency takes the place of weapon scaling attributes--strength and dex, as many of us would know them. Use a weapon type, and each kill earns you proficiency. The proficiency level of a type determines how much bonus damage you get from "high-scaling" weapons of that type. What I love about this is that you don't need to redesign your whole character just to switch from "strength" to "dex." Just use the new weapon.

Implants are how you optimize your base build--how you conform the build to your playstyle. Some can be hot-swapped in the field. Others can only be swapped out or in at the med bay. They add health, add stamina, add energy, determine how you regain health, buff your damage in certain contexts, make certain actions drain less stamina, allow you to breathe toxic gas, and on and on. Mixing and matching implants to get the most our of your build is how you build your character in The Surge. No planning necessary. I rebuilt myself entirely for the purpose of one boss fight. Then, I changed my armor and implants back to what they were, afterward, and continued on my way. It's genius. No more anxiety at the start of a game as we decide where to put our points. Those of us who built for faith in DS2 know all too well what that anxiety feels like.

This brings us to build constraints, which brings us to the power core, which brings us to tech scrap. Tech Scrap is your currency. It's what you drop when you die. It's Souls.

With tech scrap, you upgrade your power core at each zone's med bay (your bonfire). You're building only one stat in the Surge point-by-point, and this is that stat. Power Core level determines which doors you can open, how many implant slots you can use, and which implants and gear you can equip. Each implant and piece of gear carries with it a power consumption value. Total value of all equipped gear and implants must be fewer than your power core level.

[h1]The Story[/h1]

You're a guy named Warren at his first day on the job. He's starting with Creo, a technology conglomerate. At your work site, they're developing a program called "Resolve." What is it? There's your story, right there.

Shortly after you're given your exosuit, you pass out and wake up in the dumpster. Your power core is busted, so the drones were about to "disassemble" you to recycle your exosuit. Other manual laborers in exosuits are nearby, but they're homicidal monsters. What happened? There's your story, right there.

The story, by its conclusion, hit me pretty hard with two themes. The first is the feeling of powerlessness as a blue-collar laborer at a massive tech company. I found myself resenting the absolute hell out of management and feeling very anxious about the lack of information they were giving me about what was going on.

The second is environmentalism. This story, however, conveys that theme through a lens of desparation that I find very frightening. The Earth is on the verge of inability to sustain human life. How do humans react to that? Scary stuff.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

Buy this game and play it. Unless you're afraid of really goddamned hard games. Combat finds a way to be challenging even to a Dark Souls veteran. Grinding/building/leveling is all the reward with none of the hours of filler and prayer to RNGesus. And the story conveys some themes that are worth considering.

So do it. Do it now.

Do not compare with Dark Souls.
Comparing will make you disappointed.
It's a good game of its own.

[h1]In-Depth Analysis[/h1]
[h3]Pros[/h3]
[b]1.[/b]
The Surge's combat system is a breath of fresh air for the Souls genre, and even today stands out for its uniqueness, nuances and satisfactory mechanics. The limb-cutting mechanic, united with many weapons having unique powers and the implant system that allows a high customization degree about the combat approach, ensure an experience not easily replicated in other titles.

[b]2.[/b]
Each area except the first one, shares an intricate, multi-layered design that makes exploration interesting and at times, labyrinthine. Masterful shortcut placements, a metric ton of secrets and consistent design quality make each level unique in its own way, but still coherent with the global sci-fi style.

[b]3.[/b]
From heavy tanks with ample healing reserves, to agile fighters that bet everything on DPS, or tricksters that use active abilities and drones to wear enemies down, there is a play style for everyone in The Surge. The implant system is brilliant and allows players to choose what they want to prioritize in their approach, does so to a fantastic degree.

[b]4.[/b]
Replaying the game with a different weapon and/or armor class will feel like a significantly different experience, in addition NG+ mode adds some new enemies, new areas and allows further upgrades to existing weapons with previously inaccessible resources. I replayed this game six times over several years and platforms, it was always fun.

[b]5.[/b]
The implant, armor and weapon variety is really great. Around the next corner there can be a new one that can revolutionize the current build, or open a path for a completely new one. Many weapons have diverse movesets and unique powers as well, further adding to the variety, while all armors have a unique set bonus.

[h3]Cons[/h3]
[b]1.[/b]
Some weapon classes are just better than others, no matter what. For instance, Twin-Rigged and One-Handed are arguably the best, while Single-Rigged is by far the worst. Some weapon categories just become not viable against certain bosses or anyway later-game enemies. It's not impossible to finish the game with them, it's just quite depressing.

[b]2.[/b]
Dark Souls did this wrong, and Surge sadly followed: quests are obscure tasks without even a remote hint on what to do most of the time, as NPCs will spit out very vague indications of what they want. It becomes frustrating to accomplish such tasks, and the rewards are often underwhelming or plain trash.

[h1]Gameplay Breakdown[/h1]
[b]Exploration[/b]
Is performed on foot, with Warren being able to jump and leap over great distances thanks to the exoskeleton. Levels in The Surge are intricate, some of them are however definitely more complex than others. Each stage has a myriad of secret areas, hidden loot caches and even NPCs that give quests: exploring every corner, breaking all containers and taking extra time to be thorough pays off with rare gear and extra XP. As in other souls-likes there will be shortcuts to go back to the Ops Station (bonfire) more easily, however there is no fast-travel of any kind and no map.

[b]Character Management[/b]
Can be performed in a limited way while on the field, with Warren able to swap armor pieces, weapons and some implants that have the "Hot Swap" propriety, without returning to an Ops Station. The bulk of management, upgrading and crafting is however done at such safe areas, that always have a Medical Bay to replenish healing items, change Implants, use Scrap (souls) to level-up Warren. The Assembly Station allows crafting armor pieces among the known blueprints, and also upgrade weapons and armor using the resources obtained from slain enemies or found in the world. Most blueprints for gear and weapons are gained by severing enemy limbs, defeating bosses and less commonly, exploring the world.

Implants need a special mention, as they are modules that can be inserted in the Exo-Rig to give Warren passive and active abilities. Each implant costs a certain amount of Core Power (character level) to be equipped, with the total level acting as a cap to balance things out. Armor pieces also cost some Core Power to equip, usually heavier armors will cost more.

[b]Combat[/b]
Plays out in third-person, mostly in melee. Warren can wield one of five weapon categories, ranging from the slow but powerful Heavy Duty to the nimble Twin Rigged. Using a weapon class will upgrade its Proficiency level as more enemies are slain, granting bonuses - sticking to one weapon class for the whole game is recommended. Most enemies' individual limbs can be targeted to inflict different effects, stability loss and amounts of damage. The goal is performing an Execution, that will kill the enemy and sever that limb, awarding Warren with the armor worn on it and eventually their weapon, if that limb held one. A unique approach that makes any new enemy encounter exciting.

As in most souls-games, combat uses a stamina system and is highly punishing, as even common enemies can deliver great amounts of damage. Dodging at the right times, learning attack patterns and being quick-witted are the cardinal points. The more enemies are killed in a row without using an Ops Station, the higher a passive Multiplier will get, awarding bonus Scrap and even some healing recharges at random. Energy is another parameter accumulated with successful blows, and is used to fuel active implants and drone weapons, but depletes over time. Counter attacks are present. however they're a marginal mechanic simply not worth using over a dodge. All bosses have a secret way to be killed, that will award an upgraded version of their Boss Weapon, that has unique powers and is usually formidable.

[h1]Overview[/h1]
[i]The Surge[/i] is third-person action-RPG developed by Deck13 and released in 2017. Get in the shoes of Warren, a crippled man looking for a way to restore his body by signing with a corporation called CREO. As disaster surged from the depths of the CREO factory complex, Warren must try to survive amidst endless onslaught from maddened people and robots. Overall, the game managed to establish itself among its competitors by creating an interesting sci-fi world and innovative dismemberment mechanic. 

[h1]The Good[/h1]
[list]

[*] Dismemberment is a unique and brilliant mechanic.
[*] Good level design with shortcuts, well-hidden secrets and worthwhile rewards.
[*] The bosses are fun, challenging but fair even if they require some trials and errors.
[*] Fresh setting and world crafted with great art direction.
[/list]

[h1]The Bad[/h1]
[list]

[*] Lack of enemy variety. Most enemies are humanoid with the same weapons that are available to the players. 
[*] Balance issue. Either it  have sudden difficulty spikes in some areas, or the game becomes very easy with the right upgrades. Some weapons are useless.
[/list]

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Structurally, [i]The surge[/i] follows a typical souls-like formula. The core loop of the game is exploring the level while fighting enemies, reach a safe area. [i]The Surge[/i] differentiates itself by introducing a locational damage and dismemberment system that is well-implemented and satisfying when executed.  

[b][u]Combat[/u][/b]

Instead of light or heavy attacks like the game’s source inspiration [i]Dark Souls[/i], this game separates its basic attacks into vertical and horizontal attacks. Players can chain both types of attacks and execute combos alongside sliding and jumping attacks. This mechanic is important due to the location-specific damage system.

In combat, Warren can target specific locations of most enemies’ bodies. One usage of the mechanic is targeting unarmored parts of their bodies to do more damage. The second usage is by damaging an armored part, Warren can perform an execution attack that severs their limbs. By severing limbs, enemies will drop the part of their armor that can be used to obtain schematics or parts to upgrade your own armor.

[i]The Surge[/i] has really good and satisfying combat. The controls are responsive, and with 5 types of weapons, and various armors players can build Warren however they are comfortable with. The only problem with combat is there just aren’t enough  enemy varieties. Most of the enemies are humanoid with the same weapon types that players can use, and their movesets are quite limited. There are some unique humanoid type enemies that carry unique equipments that usually have unique moves and fun to fight. 

[b][u]Progression[/u][/b]

Warren can get stronger by upgrading his suit’s power core. It can be upgraded by collecting scrap parts from enemies. Upgrading it  will increase its capacity and allows you to equip better armor and unlock more implant slots. Implants are basically “skills” that can be equipped and build your character as you like. They have various effects from scaling up HP, healing, increasing your stamina and many others. They are the core of building the character in the game. 

The second progression system is equipment. There are several types of armor sets and various weapons Warren can get. A complete armor set will give him special effects that will further determine your build. They can also be upgraded with parts enemies drop. There are 5 weapon types in the game. By using a weapon from a certain category, Warren will gain proficiency that will increase your damage with said weapon types.

The progression system in the game is quite streamlined as players don’t have to worry about specific attributes or skill level. It is still quite flexible and Warren can be moulded to your liking. In my experience, this system allows experimentation with several different types of builds as there are no permanent stats tied to it. I pretty much tried all weapon types at the first half of the game before deciding to pick a favorite. There are some balance problem like some weapons can be utterly useless or one type of build is more effective than the other. 

[b][u]Exploration and Loot[/u][/b]

The levels of [i]The Surge[/i] are good, although they never really reach the same heights as the original [i]Dark Souls[/i] level. Each level is a separate area with a transition loading screen between them that makes the CREO factory complex doesn’t feel as grand and interconnected as Lordran. 

Enemies and loot are hand placed in the world. They are generally well-placed and well-thought, that makes every encounter unique and loot are worth digging nooks and crannies for. Generally I have no problem with the level design. It could be better, but I am satisfied with it. 

[h1]Technical Issue and Performance[/h1]
[u]Specs: GTX 1080, AMD Ryzen 3700x, 16 GB RAM, 1440 60 Hz[/u]

The game runs full 60 FPS almost all the time. It dipped below 60 is in the end of the game where a specific enemy type appears. This enemy's effects caused the performance to drop. Overall the game is polished at the time I played. It is bug free, aside from minor problems like characters clipping into objects. One bug that annoyed me is when a loot dropped outside of reach.

[h1]Story[/h1]
In the far future where Earth is on the brink of destruction, one man built a company with the promise of repairing a broken planet. When everything went wrong, the player as Warren is caught in the midst of it and must survive against the horde of rogue machineries and find out what happened. 

I like [i]The Surge[/i]’s story. It uses a hands-off method of story telling where the plot isn’t directly told through dialogue and cutscene but through environment design and audiologs. The setting is unique for this genre. While the theme and concept has been done before, the central mystery drove me forward and made me want to know what happened. 

[h1]Graphics and Visual[/h1]
[i]The Surge[/i] managed to build a unique world, and CREO feels like it has a personality of its own. The environment design, weapons, armor and enemies model mostly look good. Some of the locations might look the same as players spend the majority of their playtime indoors in industrial type areas but it feels appropriate to the setting where the game takes place. 

The animations are well done. Each weapon animation feels unique, they have different kill animations and combos. There isn't that much variety, but what is available is pretty good, don’t feel too janky. Overall the graphics won’t blow any minds, but it is not ugly and still carries the atmosphere and tone quite well.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2102926433

[h1]Audio and Music[/h1]
The soundtrack isn’t really anything to write home about. There isn’t any bombastic boss battle music or epic orchestration, the music mostly are just ambient sounds. I might be in the minority here, but I like the song Prisoner by Stumfol that plays in the medical area. Otherwise the music in the game is mostly ignorable. 

While the music is lacking, the soundscape of the game is very well done. A lot of effects can be heard from the hydraulics inside Warren and the enemies’ exosuits to electricity buzzing in the distance. Everything feels heavy, metallic and it fit for the game’s industrial environment. 

[h1]Conclusions[/h1]
[i]The Surge[/i] is a solid entry to the souls-like genre. It managed to differentiate itself through its innovative mechanics and unique setting. While there is always room for improvement  mainly in variety, and balance [i]The Surge[/i] is still worth your time and money if you are a fan of souls-like genre.

+ Unique limb-mechanic is a fun scavenger hunt for new equipment; makes finding new enemies enjoyable.

   + Combat is fast and smooth, with enjoyable weapon animations that have a solid hit behind them. Great finishers as well.

   + Each weapon type has an incredible variety of different chain moves that are fun to discover and utilize.

   + Implant system gives a lot of choice and variety to your build, and has quite a large variety (though I can't speak to the usefulness of many choices). Feels like a souls ring system expanded to be the main aspect of build customization.

   + Changing implants on the fly, easily acquirable materials for weapon and body upgrades, and weapon-type based bonuses that are easy to level make for a fluid change between builds and encourages experimentation.

   + I was worried about the story going in, it screamed US Michael Bay-style action movie, but came out with my expectations devoured. Strong character writing, presentation, and a consuming plot all are well done and feel a good tad closer to actual souls storytelling than I expected, but without abstract writing or certain soul-internal concepts.

   + Level design blew me away; while most of the game is inspired by Dark Souls 2, even development starting nearly after 2's release, the wrapping structure and backdoor-metroidvania take heavily from Dark Souls 1. The first time I found a shortcut right back to the "bonfire" equivalent, I was blown away, as was I every time thereafter.


   ~ Full gear sets reward the player with unique stat bonuses while wearing all of the gear. I have never enjoyed mechanics like these, as I feel it messes up both variety and character customization. However, certain global set pieces found in the DLCs lessen this issue slightly, and the popularity of these mechanics in jrpgs and the like lead to believe many enjoy this, so may not be a negative for some.

   ~ Completely lacks online play, co-op or pvp or otherwise. Not entirely negative, as build variety wouldn't really be great enough to encourage this anyway, and the game feels cinematic in a certain way where it would be fairly odd. Still, it's missing presence can be felt at times, and would have contributed to some degree of further play.

   ~ Since many of the generic enemies wield the same weapon types as you, as that is where you get those weapons from, they do use the same movesets as you as well. This means there's a sort of a closeness between you and them combat-wise which can feel jarring, but it does lead to a nice feeling of knowing exactly what they're capable of doing, even if you are not entirely familiar with them.


   - Weapon variety is low, considering the difference between the majority of the weapons of the same type is just stats and appearance.

   - Implant system and upgrades are essentially the only form of level and power progression; a complete lack of soulslike jrpg-inspired stats. Despite the addition of implants, builds tend to feel linear, and experimentation is not as wide as could be.

   - Along with the lack of stats is a lack of magic or other secondary means of combat. Greatly contributes to linearity.

   - Some level of lesser variety in enemies exists, and becomes more apparent the further in you go. Different enemy types are dropped in occasionally to spruce it up, but you can often tell when you've fought the same enemy so many times.

   - Certain bugs exist mechanically, and others exist that can block you out of certain character questlines entirely (or this may have just been an odd choice related to character dialogues, but that would be a negative as well). However, these are not incredibly prevalent.

   - Because of prior issues mentioned with variety in build, the replayability takes a great detriment. I did many different runs through my time with each souls game, but the difference in my hours between the games speak for themselves.



Despite some issues I mentioned that are directly tied to the positives, this game is more than worth your time and money. I didn't even mention the money above, but this game is an absolute and complete bargain at only $15 (though, as I mentioned, the DLC is well worth your time, but is some more on top). Absolutely recommended for fans of soulslikes who can handle some level of jank, but may want to reconsider if you're a particular fan of magic or other similar builds.
