Alright, so first off I want to say I have a bias towards games like this. I have spent many hours in DS, DS2, DS2 scholar, DS3, Bloodborne, and Lords of the Fallen. I recently beat the surge after 21hrs of gameplay so now I think I can give my opinion.

This game has some of the most fun combat I have ever seen in this type of game. Pulling or cutting someones limbs off for their gear is simply fantastic each time. The jumping and ducking mechanic when used on certain enemies feels incredibly rewarding when pulled off. However, this game has 2 glaring problems that makes it more of a chore than entertaining.

The first deals with the enemies themselves, now there are alot of LOTF esk features in this game such as The Champions rage bar, the "soul" multiplier, and the reviving enemies. However, this game has the exact opposite problem LOTF had. LOTF had really simplistic enemy designs with basic attack patterns (Think Dark Souls Lite) but its bosses seemed cheap and unfair at times usually leading you to cheese them out to progress. The Surge has the most ridiculous mobs I have ever seen. Most of the mobs in this game can 1 shot you regardless of armor (have tested fully upgraded LYNX and RHINO, on average the RHINO can sustain 1-2 more hits with a HUGE movement penalty). The bosses however are pretty fun, a little predictable but a fight you know will be tough but can still come out the victor. (Except 1 boss, random camera angle switch? What is this Nier Automata? lol)

 Most of the small enemies are 10x tougher than ANY boss in this game and even other DS titles. Imagine if all the small mobs in bloodborne were replaced with Gascoigne (If any of u have played bloodborne). Its cool at first but after a while it becomes tedious to die to a new enemy youv'e never seen and have to fight ALL the mobs to get back to one guy and figure out in 3 secs what he did to kill you and how to dodge it. Im NOT against fighting an enemy multiple times to figure out how he works and eventually defeat him but if I have to fight 30 Gascoignes to get to the ONE guy I wanna fight it becomes very unfun. This leads me to the Duck/Jump feature. This feature works on 2 enemies throughout the entire game. Ones a Mini boss and the other is a regular mob. Pulling off one of these moves during an enemies attack and pushing in for a stun is fantastic! It makes you feel incredible, but it is utterly useless since you are given so much stamina that dodging left or right is safer and more consistant (Think of bloodborne... wow this game is kinda like that in terms of movement). 

The second one I probably should have mentioned first but Im not re-typing this thing. The main problem with this game is the actual level design. I dont mean the interconnectivity, ive always enjoyed interwoven maps. I mean the color/art behind it. All of the areas minus the first and part of the... third I think... are the same mechanical industrial factories. Now I KNOW this is the style they are going for but to connect all the areas they use "tunnels" with lifts and doorways. The problem is the tunnels all have the same black tunnel/yellow guard rail design. They are almost impossible to tell apart from one another especially the dim lit ones. So on top of having to retrieve your lost "souls" from the new guy that one shot you while you were blocking, you have to navigate endless coridors all the same color and figure out where the fuck to go. I really would have loved these tunnels to be color coded (think mirrors edge style) so I could tell one areas tunnels from the next since they are in all the areas. Ill be honest, the caticombs in LOTF was my least favorite area in the game, it was very similar in design and I would get lost down there all the time (Im not the best navigator) but I have completed all the DS games including bloodborne without an issue so im not that bad. Besides DS2, I did look up a guide for that one... Anyway Ill wrap this up with the pro's in a final thoughts paragraph and TL:DR for those that dont wanna read this... I know I wouldnt.

Final Thoughts (MY OPINION): This game has ALOT to offer with fleshed out combat, an interesting world, and weird people you meet along the way. Its problems  lie in its repetitive art design/impossibly hard to navigate levels (Though I am not the best navigator), along with standard mobs that could be end game bosses. I really enjoyed the first 10 hrs of this game up until the 2nd boss. The weapons were interesting although few in nature along with armor sets not really giving you much in terms of actual armor lol. The injections/implants system is a really cool idea that kinda changes up the way you play without having to include a class system. All-in-all if you guys loved bloodborne/a really fast DS than this game might be for you. I would wait for a sale tho, as someone who isnt very good but has played all the DS games, I beat this in 21hours when most of that was me trying to navigate the nightmare hellscape that is The Surge. I would wait for a sale, this game was fun but not $50 fun. Its definitly better than lords of the fallen but id wait till its around $30. I doubt Ill go back to it unless they add some different or more interesting weapons and maybe tone down the 1 shots. Also PC port is good! I5 and 1060.

TL:DR- This game is essentially SciFi BloodBorne, Fast satisfying combat, Fun Bosses, Interesting story, Regular mobs that can out DPS all the bosses in this game, and hard to navigate levels due to repetitive art (could be me though). I think $30 is a good price.

I recently finished my first playthrough of The Surge, and I’m working my way through NG+. It’s an excellent game, equal in quality to any other Souls-like experience I've had (as good as Nioh, even…in my opinion). It has several unique twists and additions to the traditional Souls-like mechanics. 

The most interesting new mechanic to me is the surplus energy meter that’s included in the health/stamina HUD. The energy meter sort of operates like a combo meter, in that it builds up with successful strikes and then depletes over time. However, it causes you to constantly make mid-combat decisions between harvesting parts and “potion-free healing,” depending upon which implants you equip. In other words, when the surplus energy bar is charged enough, you have a choice between using that energy to execute a finishing move (and thereby have a chance at harvesting the enemy armor part you were targeting during combat, not to mention a guaranteed end to the skirmish) or using that energy to heal, and thereby save your limited supply of healing injectables for later. Theoretically, a good enough player could have infinite healing power just by managing surplus energy well.The surplus energy-based healing injectable mechanic feels a lot like the Ki Pulse in Nioh; it's a pretty addictive combat mechanic once you've got the rhythm down.

Another mechanic I've noticed involving surplus energy is the potential loss of souls upon death. In The Surge, you have a limited amount of time to return to the scene of your demise in order to reclaim your souls. The clock starts ticking when you exit the save/upgrade zone. However, more time gets added to the clock if you successfully execute a finishing move, so this may force you to spend healing injectables instead of surplus energy in order to give yourself more time to get back to your at-risk souls.

Movement and combat is fluid and feels natural (i.e. this game is nothing like Deck 13’s prior Souls-like attempt, and they clearly learned a lot after LOTF). The graphics are great, and the environmental ambiance is extremely well-done (albeit somewhat repetitive). I personally like the song that plays incessantly in the save/upgrade zones, but it would be nice if this could be changed up in the options or a mod (Edit: you can! There's a "songs" folder in the game files where you can upload a .WAV file of any song you like. Now the Medbay plays Zeppelin's No Quarter, and this small change had a pretty radical effect on the feeling in the game).

The one major complaint I would have about this game is the way implants are managed and used, which is really clunky. There’s no reason they couldn’t have made it easier to sort and arrange the various injectables that are available in the game, all of which have very similar icons and colors so its very hard to go through and select between them. When you do have multiple injectables equipped, they are all on the same button, so it’s difficult to cycle through and select them. Particularly so, given that you don't get a moment's peace during any single one of the combat scenarios, so this forces you to be really quick and precise when deploying consumables. They should have just used a traditional consumables selection and equipping interface. 

A more minor complaint is the absence of backstory and lore. The events that led to the state of the game's world really deserve some exposition, and there were plenty of missed opportunities to provide that to us. NPCs have little dialogue or interactive value...they seem as clueless as we are about what caused all this chaos and mutation. Granted, you don't play a Souls-like for explicitly narrated storylines. But, here, Deck 13 was able to create a unique and curious sci-fi world, and even built in all the story mechanisms that would have been needed to tell the backstory (i.e. left-behind emails and journal entries from victims of the incident, and NPC dialogue options). But they didn't deliver on the story to bring it home. They could have taken some queues from Horizon Zero Dawn in this area. If they continue with this IP, I think some lore and backstory would go a long way to give the game a timeless nature (maybe even a prequel DLC for starters?).

The bosses seem pretty fair, but really most enemies in the game are hard. The enemy leveling gets more progressive on NG+ (as described a little more below), but the first playthrough isn't very forgiving. You need to focus on upgrading equipment and weapon proficiency to make it fun. That’s probably intentional, given that they have a parts harvesting mechanic that is very integral to the combat system, so farming and upgrading seems to be intended as a core player objective here.

The NG+ game is very well-thought out, and clearly reflects the developer’s intent to present a new experience for players who have beaten the game. In a very interesting twist, the game seems to have added significant defense and damage to some of the enemies, but left the others alone, so now levels feel a lot more like Bloodborne’s set of tiered enemy capabilities (and less like a game that is nothing but bosses and mini-bosses, which is how I felt throughout first several hours of playing Surge).

Overall, I’d say this is one of my favorite gaming experiences, and I’m pretty surprised that this game isn’t as popular, widely discussed, and highly rated as Nioh in the Souls fan community. I’ll close by saying that I highly, highly recommend “TotalBiscuit’s thoughts on The Surge” for a brilliant and scholarly nearly-hour-long analysis of this game.

TLDR:  The surge is not bad per se. I would actually say the first half of the game is pretty decent. After that, however the game falls apart rapidly and becomes a massive, frustrating mess. This,and a series of absolutely baffling design decisions make me not want to recommend this game.

This game prides itself in being a hardcore action RPG with high difficulty in a sci fi setting. And for the first two areas that formula works rather well. You dodge the mad shells that were you collegues, swinging around industrial equipment, chopping off body parts in a sprawling environment that invites you to explore and finding shortcuts that take you back to the ops that act as checkpoint. That part is fun.

As soon as you kill the first boss however you will realize that your enemies suddenly got massively upgraded. They no longer stagger. Their attacks will kill you in 1-2 hits. Their health pools got inflated. This sadly is the theme for the rest of the game. Your enemies' power level will rapidly increase while the growth of your character is heavily gated by upgrade materials. Leveling up your power core will barely do anything for you. This will lead to weird situation where you wail on your enemies with an industrial hammer the size of a man and barely scratching them only for them to power through your onslaught and deliver an enemic looking kick that will drain about 80% of your health.Sounds about right.

Speaking of enemy power- it is hillarious how effective their armor is. Armored body parts will gain up to 60% damage reduction and higher stagger resistance. This actually plays very well into this game's main mechanic of targeting specific body parts, as it directly encourages you to actively go for unarmored spots. This only gets incredibly weird when you get your hands on those armor pieces, and all of a sudden a piece of protective gear that could stop anti armor weaponry beforehand now has the defensive capabilities of a wet sheet of paper.

Damage in itself is also handled rather poorly. Dmaage types are split into three different physical attributes and a somewhat enigmatic 'elemental' stat. Elemental covering everyting from toxic gas to getting set on fire.  Since phyiscal attacks are allways a mix of all three damage types ,there is no real feedback to which physical damage types are more efficient against which enemies, making the distinction somehwat pointless. Not as pointless as the elemental damage stat however. You see- the first wepaons that will deal elemental damage are available pretty much after you beat the second boss. On twin rigged and staff type weapons which most people wont have used extensively. Also it is AT THIS VERY POINT the game will throw mostly robots and humans in HAZMAT suits at you. Both of which are highly resistant to elemental damage.

Level design also takes a massive nose dive after the second boss. Open areas get traded for series of linear corridors with the occasional box shaped room thrown in. With the occasional really bad misstep. Like that one instance where a shortcut back from ops will lead you onto a small patch of dirt surroudned by acid and enemy ambushes waiting on both sides. Also enemy placement tends to go a bit overboard later on, making you fight groups of enemeis that can kill you with 2-3 hits frequently. This,paired with very long walks makes getting back to a point you died at a chore.  After dying you will, as it is expected of these types of game, drop all of your currency which you can pick back up when you get to where you died. For some reason the devs decided to add a timer of 2 Minutes and 30 seconds to this process. If that timer runs out, your scrap is invariably lost. Between this and the massive amount of slow but powerful enemies, you will soon realize that simply running through the and ignoring a lot of the encounters is the best way to progress through the later levels. Also, expect a lot of 'lunge ambushes' where an enemy is covneniently placed out of your view behind some boxes or a doorframe only for the to hit you with a very powerful unblockable lunge attack if you walk past them. This is realtively likely to outright kill you. Dying to those allways feels incredibly cheap, but every area has at least one of those hidden somewhere.

The area where this game fails the msot however,are its bosses. Only one of them is somewhat decent. There is only five of them in the entire game. And one of them is used twice. But in hindisght that might have been for the best, as the ones they did come up with are all among the worst bosses i have ever fought. Every single one of them has periods of invulnerability where you need to wail on some part- or in one case another enemy entirely- in order to even make the boss vulnerable. This serves only to drag the fight out as long as possible. To add insult to injury here, every boss also deals massive damage to the point of them easily oneshotting you. Every single boss encoutner feels like a long, drawn out grind only designed to tire the player out until they make a simple mistake that immediately kills them. They aren't tests of skill but rather long, drawn out contests of atrition. And if that wasn't bad enough, every single boss also has a hidden prerequisite you have to fulfill in order to get their best weapon drop, which msotly consists of the player handycapping themselves.

All in all- the game confuses being 'hard' with incredibly handycapping the player and making them jump through tedious and frustrating hoops. There was potential in the beginning but terrible boss fights and a large amount of cheap deaths sour the experience to the point of it turning into a slow and frustrating grind.

[h1][b]Recommendation:[/b][/h1]
Would I recommend the game? I would. This isn't a bad little game, especially for a souls-like. It is on the easier side, and while it's not an amazing game with deep, well-crafted mechanics, it was fun for the time I spent with it. That said, it is not without its faults, and I do think there are a decent number of issues that, if addressed, could have made this game something really special.

Firstly, the visuals are really great. I love the way this game looks. The handcrafted environments and enemy designs give it a great aesthetic, although I would have liked a bit more enemy variety. It gives me strong Dead Space vibes in terms of the setting, but with a much lighter tone.

While the areas are fairly small, the connecting corridors, unlockable shortcuts and train system all help give the game a nice flow.

The sound design and audio throughout the game were good for what they were. The voice acting was also done well with the material the actors had to work with. I just think the writing itself needed to be more compelling.

On that note, the narrative is a big issue for me. It is basically non-existent, and while I understand they were going for a more typical souls-like experience where the story isn't handed to you and you discover things as you go, I just don't think it was done well.

The start is strong. It's interesting, and you genuinely want to learn more. But from that very first cutscene where you choose your starting gear, it feels like the game suddenly jumps ahead without giving you enough backstory, setting or context. This continues throughout the experience, with NPCs not really telling you much, and the audio logs and environmental storytelling also not giving you enough to really piece things together.

I understand what they were trying to achieve, but I don't think they found the right balance between what to tell you, when to tell you, and how to tell it. Which sucks, because this is a really interesting IP that I would genuinely like to learn more about.

For me, a masterclass example of this would be the first Dead Space. You go onto the Ishimura on a mission without really knowing what to expect, then discover what has happened as you progress. You slowly piece everything together, and it's done in a compelling way. That's something I just didn't get here. Instead, this game leaves you feeling more lost than intrigued.

The gameplay is also very hit and miss. I played the entire game on controller, and for the most part, that was fine. The biggest issue, which I hope they ironed out in the subsequent game, is the lock-on camera. This makes combat extremely annoying and much more frustrating than it needs to be.

You can't block properly unless you're locked on to the enemy that is hitting you, selecting which limb to target sometimes doesn't work well, and swapping between enemies is also very annoying. All of this makes fighting multiple enemies a massive pain, to the point where you'll often want to fight them one at a time for most of the game. This makes the game go very slowly, especially since whenever you "rest" or use the crafting/med station, every normal enemy respawns. Bosses and mini-bosses are the exceptions. So, the biggest issue I had with the game was definitely the camera during combat.

The combat mechanics themselves were OK. I liked the different phases of the bosses, but they were all very similar and didn't have much variety in their movesets between phases, which made them very easy. Personally, I thought the normal enemies throughout the game were harder than most of the bosses.

If the bosses had more diverse movesets that they switched between, making the fights a little less predictable, I think they would have been much more enjoyable. But for what they are, I thought they were fine.

Switching between limbs and targeting armoured or unarmoured parts was cool in concept, just a little finicky in practice. I did like the idea of cutting off limbs to get blueprints for new gear, although I think it would have been cooler if you salvaged the equipment directly from the enemy rather than needing to craft it afterwards. Something more like actually taking the gear from them.

When it comes to the DLC, I thought [i]The Good, the Bad and the Augmented[/i] was pretty mediocre. It is essentially just completing missions with modifiers applied, and I personally found it uninteresting.

However, [i]A Walk in the Park[/i] was a completely different story and one I very much enjoyed. It gives you more backstory about how you ended up there and what was going on, while the DLC's setting and gameplay were just really fun.

The only issue I had with it was that I tackled it towards the end of the game. By that point, it was very easy, and story-wise it didn't really make much sense for where I was in the main game. Again, the pacing felt a bit off. But besides its placement in the overall experience, I really enjoyed it.

Overall, it's not a bad game, just not a great or particularly memorable one. If you're looking for a souls-like on the easier side to try out, this isn't a bad pick-up. I think the base price is fine for what you get, although you'll probably want the two DLCs mentioned above. Because of that, I would consider getting everything as a bundle. As this is an older game and it goes on a decent discount, I'd recommend waiting until then to pick it up.

Deck13 doesn't appear to have learned much of anything from Lords of the Fallen. 

The Surge has a competently designed world and story. Exploring and learning what's going on in the game is engaging and entertaining. Most of the environments nail the interconnected, shortcut littered style that Dark Souls fans enjoy. Some of them are a bit samey and mazelike in construction, which can make exploring a chore, but overall I liked them. 

The combat is another story. Most enemies have unreasonable amounts of poise, and most encounters are single humanoid enemies at a time. You will do your forward dodge attack, then dodge back, repeatedly, to kill most enemies.  Enemy attacks typically have too much horizontal tracking, ambiguous hurtboxes, and low startup to do much of anything else. The forward dodge attack for most weapon types does significant damage, has a fast startup, and a fast recovery. Many enemies utilize the same kinds of weapons and attacks, including some bosses, making combat pretty samey overall throughout the game, with a few exceptions.
Compounding this, there are only five weapon types in the game. Though there are many weapons of each individual type, they're more or less just superior or inferior versions of one-another. Due to the way damage scaling occurs, you're disincentivized from trying different weapon types, because your proficiency will be low and require grinding to get back up to par. 
The armor selection is pretty varied, but most pieces offer little additional protection in exchange for significantly hampering your character. There are some locations where the Liquidator (basically a biohazard suit) set is helpful to negate environmental damage, but otherwise I saw no reason to use anything other than Lynx for the majority of the experience, aside from swapping out the arm pieces for parts of a better set towards the end of the game.

Overall I had fun with The Surge, but my time with the game was marred by several frustrating moments, including an instance where my progress was not saved upon exiting the game from the menu. I was ready for it to be done when I killed the final boss. 
If it goes on sale for less than twenty dollars, I'd encourage Souls fans looking for something to do to pick it up. Otherwise, pass.

Rating: 8/10
Genre: Third Person RPG

The Good:
+ Haunting Sci-fi atmosphere with lots of graphical options 

+ Upgrading your suit allows you to carry more ‘cores’ which means you can equip better gear and implants. 

+ A variety of different implants (perks) that you can equip that can result in many different character builds. You can equip implants that focus on health, stamina, energy, healing, damage, speed, etc.  You can be a ‘glass cannon’ or a ‘walking death tank’ by the end of the game and everything in between. 

+ Getting different armor and weapons is dependant on which body part you cut off in combat. I like the system because it provides a change from the typical finding equipment in chests. 

+ Combat has a faster pace than your typical Dark Souls game. Dodging and dashing around enemies is encouraged and leaves many enemies exposed for counter attacks. Combat has a slower feel in the beginning of the game but once you get a feel for the mechanics and weapons things become much easier. 

+ Lots of different armor and weapons that fit any particular play style. 

+ level design can be a bit confusing at first, but discovering new shortcuts always feels rewarding and encourages further exploration. 

+ The DLC ‘A walk in the park’ is an extra story expansion that takes place in an abandoned amusement park. The change of environment was nice. It adds about 4 hours of additional story content and exploration. 

+ New Game plus allows you to continue playing from the beginning with all your gear and implants carried over. 

The Average:
+/- The story is told mostly through audio logs scattered about the world. The story never feels like the focus of the game and takes a back seat to the gameplay. It doesn’t help that the main character is as charismatic as a cardboard box. 

+ The DLC’s The Good The Bad and The Augmented, is a arcade style gauntlet run where you can set different difficulty modifiers for better rewards. There are nine episodes but each episode is just a rehash of different areas mixed together. The new perks are insanely good and practically break the main game but overall, the DLC is very repetitive. 

+/- This is similar to Dark souls so expect a lot of cheap and frustrating deaths especially in the first few areas of the game. The game is very difficult in the first half of the game when you are still trying to figure things out, you will die a lot. Frustration does happen frequently in the beginning.  However, once you are able to get over the initial difficulty curve the game becomes easier and far less frustrating. 

+/- A few side quests that don’t offer any meaningful rewards and are too obtuse to complete without the help of a walkthrough.  

Conclusion:
I was one of the few that liked Deck13’s other game Lords of the Fallen. Its easy to compare this to Dark Souls, it has similar mechanics but if you look past that and appreciate the game for what it is rather than what its not, you will see a fun, challenging if not flawed game.

In the year of 2019, there are nearly hundreds of games that do their best to emulate the success, and most importantly, the fun of Dark Souls. Souls-like is a term that gets thrown around often now due to just how many games have tried to capture that feeling right, but most tend to miss the mark. Be it from a lack of proper mechanics, bland worlds or doing all they can to pad the game out as much as possible, few ever actual feel as satisfying as the ever famous Dark Souls franchise. 

The Surge, however, is a rare gem unlike much else. 

This game, Souls-like as it may be, is unique in ways all of its own that make for a truly amazing experience. Some large changes immediately noticeable come in the form of a limb removal system, giving a whole new meaning to critical hits, and even executions that will never fail to leave you ecstatic...if you're a fan of brutal kills and gore. 

On top of this, the way you modify yourself is vastly different than that of your typical Souls-like, coming in the form of mods to your suit itself. Though the progression of some of these feels rather lacking, or at the least, paced strangely, it's nothing that hinders the flow of the game. 

In the few negative reviews that you can find for this game, many point out a lack of story telling, or new features to the Souls-like genre. As for the story telling, it is, at the least, what you'd expect from a Souls-like game, while still having moments of far more head on storytelling. I can only assume those harping on the story telling aren't familiar with the genre itself. 

As for features, if the the Limb system, executions and suit modding aren't enough to warrant adding anything "new", you also gain a drone. This acts both as a weapon, and a way to gain access to secret areas when used correctly. I can only assume those complaining about a lack of new features didn't get very far.

I'm just starting my third playthrough of this game after having beaten it twice within the first 2 weeks of its release, and immediately, I'm feeling the exact same excitement that I felt my very first time. Noticing small things I didn't catch before, and of course, enjoying the change of pace where you start off in a drastically different way than most of this genre, it's all deeply refreshing. 

This is a game that I'd recommend to anyone looking for that fun mix of challenge and rewarding exploration, adding in of course some highly enjoyable gameplay, and an always welcomed, but optional grind for more power. 

Obviously, if Souls-like games aren't your cup of tea, this likely won't be either, but despite sharing such close relations, The Surge is one of few games of its kind that manages to set itself apart in a whole new way. This game is most definitely worth the price, full price or otherwise, and knowing that this game is getting a well deserved sequel warms my heart.

TL;DR: 5/10
There's some ideas here that I liked and hadn't seen in other Souls-likes - it definitely puts it's own spin on the genre - but ultimately the game feels very tedious and I just didn't have a good time, though the reasons why are largely subjective. 
I'd give it a neutral rating, but since that's not a thing on Steam, I'm leaning more towards the thumbs down.

---

Let's start with the cool stuff I quite liked:
You can target separate limbs, which will have different defences and stagger values. When you've damaged a limb enough, you can cut it off in a finishing move; collecting gear is tied to this. You unlock new pieces of armour, as well as crafting materials, by cutting them off of your foes.
When fighting robots, you don't get the limb cutting finisher, instead you can break parts during combat, actually changing the enemy's move-set and defences, which I liked a lot.

Boss fights also make use of this mechanic: It seems each of them is a bit of a gimmick fight, where you need to chop off specific limbs and the fight becomes easier as you do.
I've read people complain about this, but I personally enjoyed it. My only complaint here would be that I found the way to each boss oddly more challenging than the battle itself...

There's a more in-depth dodging mechanic as well, that allows you to duck or jump in addition to the more traditional dodging to the side.
Admittedly, I didn't find practical use cases for this, but looking through some user written guides, it seems there's a lot to learn here. So while I personally didn't play enough to master these advanced dodges, the idea intrigues me and I can see more patient folks than me getting a kick out of it.

I also would've liked to see more of the story unfold and figure out what the heck is actually happening at this strange, brainwashing company... but there's many design choices I found frustrating, that burned me out rather quickly and, for me, overshadowed the good.

---

This is where the list of The Bad™ starts.
I will preface this by pointing out that this is a very subjective list. I think most of the things that frustrated me could be exactly what would draw another player in, so decide for yourself whether or not these sound like deal breakers to you.

For one, the game is insanely punishing. 
All normal enemies kill you in 2-3 hits, upgrading armour didn't seem to make a noticeable difference, and your foes usually show up in groups, too.
To make this more problematic, you get very few healing items that - unlike in other Souls-games - don't automatically become more and stronger over time, but instead require you to give up on other upgrades if you want more healing. Your Estus equivalent here takes up an equipment slot, so either you'll be stuck with just three weak heals forever, or you have to give up on more fun upgrades that might allow you to shape your playstyle more.

Now, the game is actually surprisingly kind in that it allows you to safely stash your currency, so you can't lose it by dying anymore.
However, along with this kindness, they also added a timer to your dropped stash, should you die before you got to bank it. You get 2:30 minutes to return, else your tech scrap (the game's currency) will be lost.
This timer is extended slightly for each enemy killed, so when directly running back the exact path you previously died on, carefully clearing your path, you should arrive with plenty of extra time. Yet I felt a little robbed of some freedom to decide how I want to proceed, being forced to run head first back into trouble, into whatever I obviously struggled with, instead of being given the option to more cautiously explore to potentially find a better way... 
I'm not really sure why they decided to add this mechanic, as I think there's enough pressure in the runback to your lost loot as is, without the need to add more artificially.
This timer particularly bugged me when it came to boss fights, as it either meant to give up on my scrap, or needing to fight the boss *now*. There's no homeward bone equivalent, so once your scrap pile lands in a boss arena, it's stuck in there until you beat the boss. It also doesn't spawn at the entrance, it spawns in the exact spot you died and needing to navigate there before your timer runs out in the heat of a battle felt a little awkward.
Though ultimately, I stopped caring about the timer altogether and often just let it run out while exploring elsewhere, no longer caring for my scrap, which I don't think was the intention behind it.

This may seem like a small complaint, but navigation sucks in this game!
I don't think I've ever gotten as lost in any game as I did in this one - constantly. I thought it might be a me-issue, but reading through other people's thoughts, the confusion seems universal. It's a real pain to navigate the claustrophobic, filled with ambushes sci-fi hallways, and everywhere looks identical to each previous location!
I reckon this was a conscious decision on the designers' part, to make you uncomfortable in Creo's incredibly unwelcoming labs and add to the contradiction between all the "Creo is your awesome super rad new family that loves you"-videos playing everywhere, and the messed up stuff actually happening behind the curtains, but I can't help but feel like there would've been a healthier middle ground here, that still tells the same story but ends up being more fun to play through... 
It also made the runbacks to bosses terrible, especially since running past enemies often simply isn't an option with how little space they give you; You either arrive at the boss with some of your hard to come by healing items already used up, or fight through every enemy on each attempt anew.

There's also many mechanics that are never really explained to you. Like the aforementioned special dodges, which the tutorial tells you the controls for, but gives no example of when or why you should use them. Blocking with proper timing uses less stamina, gathering enough scrap to level up refills your healing items, you can decide to use either horizontal or vertical attacks, but I couldn't notice any effective difference between the two and the game never tells you... There's a lot of depth here that I wish were explained better (or at all).

---

Ultimately, while there were more things I personally disliked than enjoyed, I can't call The Surge a bad game.
It seems a well polished product with a lot of thought and care poured into it, that manages to create a very different experience than other games of the genre. Though I think this last point might be exactly why many people - myself included - never quite warmed up to it. 
If you want a more traditional Souls-like, this is not it and I'm not sure you'd enjoy it. If you want to see a new take on the genre however - and are perhaps a little more patient than me - give it a shot!

PROS:

1. Visual design of armour, enemies, bosses, environment is simply a HELL YEAH moment for anyone enjoying the cyborg aesthetic. It looks an feels COOL

2. Finishing animations are one of the best in (non-slasher) soulslikes that I have seen, feel very satisfying and not like a waste of time

3. Some really refreshing and original combat / upgrade systems are introduced in this game - targeting different body parts, energy system in addition to regular stamina

4. Classic linear soulslike level design with unlockable shortcuts, exploring is payed off with upgrades and weapons

5. Good variety of attacks ensures combat doesn't get too stale during the game duration - horizontal and vertical attacks with separate binds, sprint attack, jump attack, block counter, dive counter, drone attack

CONS:

1. Boss fights are pretty unintuitive and janky - you often need to attack specific part of boss model at specific time in order to deal damage and move to the next part of the fight. 

2. Dodging attacks is pretty consistent, but blocking isn't - some attacks have weird hitbox and might reach you anyway. Perfect blocking is not rewarding, since if you miss it, enemies can drain you stamina and kill you way too easily. 

3. There is no "real" map in the game and it is very easy to get lost in dozens of identical looking tunnels and shafts. There is no quick travel and getting back to early locations once you reach the level required to get late-game lootrooms there is so tedious that I didn't even bother with it.

OVERALL:

If you are tired of fantasy-themed soulslikes and seeing the same 3 mechanics, love the challenge and the futuristic cyber vibe, definitely give it a try!

[b][h1] 8/10 great souls futuristic game [/h1][/b]
[b]TLDR at the end.[/b]
[h3] Difficulty [/h3] 
This game starts very slow and VERY hard but it gradually makes you more powerful with the upgrades you find and unlock, becoming extremely fun and addictive as you feel the power spike with each new upgrade or weapon. And at the end you're just a killing machine and barely ever dying.

I beat all Dark Souls games and Elden Ring, and thought this was going to be easy, but no, the beginning for sure is challenging and you won't make it far if you face-tank every enemy. [b] So take your time in the early game.[/b]
 
The biggest difference is that you have 1 single "bonfire" base where you upgrade and respawn per location, but the good thing that you need to understand early on is that everytime you go somewhere "too far" from your base, there is always a shortcut that leads right into your "bonfire" to reduce backtracking. You can have very big location with a single base but about 5 shortcuts to it from the different areas, so the map design is god tier.

[h3] Mid-End Game and DLC [/h3] 
The mid and end game are amazing, progress is very noticeable and cutting off limbs to get the gear pieces is extremely well done and satisfying!

The DLCs complement the game perfectly and I recommend you do them alongside your playthrough as they give you great powerful gear and are well balanced in terms of difficulty. The DLCs won't allow you to progress in them faster than in the main game story because they are meant so that you do them along-side the main game (do not leave them to the end as you won't be able to come back to them if you beat the last boss of the main game).

[h3] The only downside [/h3] 
The only possible down side I see here is that you have "weapon proficiency" that levels up the more you use a weapon type, so in the mid-end game, this makes switching to a newly found weapon feel always underwhelming if the weapon is from a different weapon type.

And also expensive weapon/armor upgrades, so whenever you find a new cool weapon that is your same weapon type you can't really test how good it is as it's not upgraded as high as your main weapon, and getting it max level is expensive (and very limiting of resources if going Mk.5).
You can probably upgrade to the very max level about 2 full gear sets and 2 weapons if you find all the Nano Cores which is the only material used for max level up and it's not farmable.
So you have so much cool weapon and gear variety but you rarely switch anything as it's expensive to do so.

Note: Your gear has "gearset bonus" for when you wear all 5 pieces of the same gear type/name that you don't ever know what it is unless you craft the whole gearset, wear it and check the bonus in your stats. So I recommend you google the gearset bonuses before crafting the gear.

Also, the game is very polished and far ahead any early-access titles you see these days.

 [h2] TLDR [/h2] 
• Game very good. Starts very hard, gets much better as you upgrade your gear and character.
• Your "bonfire" base is only 1 per level and you have multiple shortcuts to it from the whole map.
• DLCs are good and balanced and should be done alongside the game.
• Weapon/gear switching after upgraded is underwhelming because of limited upgrade materials.
• Google Gearset bonuses before crafting the gearsets.
• Game very polished

[b] Is The Surge a perfect game? [/b]
No.

[b] Is The Surge as terrible as so many people claim it to be? [/b]
Absolutely not.

[b]This might be one of the most overhated games I've ever played[/b] And honestly.. I have no idea why that is as the game itself is solid for the most part.
[b] The only complaint I have is the level design,[/b] which is very confusing in some areas, but that is about the only negative I can think of.

[h1]The Positives[/h1]
[b] > The game offers many possible builds [/b] with the implants mechanic, many different weapons and 3 different types of armor (light,medium and heavy) which all can change the way you approach encounters.

[b] > Combat is responsive and has a feeling of weight to it,[/b] which in turn makes the combat more satisfying. 
Unlike Dark Souls' dodge rolls you have a side step dodge, which has very minimal iframes so using block is crucial in many situations when dodging isn't ideal or possible (in cramped spaces). 
In addition to stamina there is also energy, which can be altered with implants (for buffs at high energy levels) and is also used for executions, which sever enemy body parts and this is the main way of acquiring new armor pieces and weapons.
Targeting different body parts can give you an advantage in battle as targeting unarmored body parts will deal much more damage.

[b] > Boss design for the most part is very solid [/b] and all the fights are fairly balanced (no one shot mechanics for example). Firebug is definitely a standout imo.

[b] > Game progression and overall difficulty ramp up are both well paced [/b] and I never felt like I was put into an unfair situation.

[b] > Map exploration is rewarding [/b] and you can gain an edge by finding better implants, scrap (souls) and new weapons. There are also a few side-quests you can take part in for some substantial rewards.

[h1] In conclusion[/h1]
Yes, the game took more than a few ideas from Dark Souls, but if you're looking for another Dark Souls game then look elsewhere.
The Surge stands out as it's own kind of game and if you won't respect it's rules, you will be punished for it.

The Good:
-The high level concept was great. Defeat your opponents, use their stuff to progress.
-Every enemy is a serious challenge
-I honestly enjoyed running around exploring

The Okay:
-The combat system is... okay. When I started the blocking option didn't work, and more often than not I was winning by luck more than anything.

The Bad:
-Too few enemy types/exoframes. There are around six of them, which is dissipointing.
-Weapons are designed in a fashion which rewards you with extra damage for using them. Which takes away any desire to swap to different weapons. Why would I switch to a new weapon which does significantly less damage? I used the weapon from the first boss until the end of the game.
-I hated the bosses. I never found them fun, and without a guide I just got my ass handed to me. Honestly they felt like a punishing roadblock to the only part of the game I liked, exploring.
-The story.... oh god.... I know people rave about the style of storytelling in the Dark Souls series. Where you have to learn what's going on by reading absolutly everything and you never get any real answers to everything.
For some people this is immersive, and realistic.
For me? I found it lazy and forgettable.
Upon the start of the game you know only that something went wrong, everybody seems to be completely insane (except the security?), and that you need to get to the main boardroom where all the answers will be revealed.
After you get to that point the only person who regularly talks to you... stops. You're given no answers, and bizzarely you're expected to continue on to trying to stop a rocket launch but nobody bothers to tell you why.
The secret experiments they're doing are barely hinted at, nobody botheres to explain what happened (in fact everybody asked says "I don't know what happened." Everybody!)

So why am I ripping on the story so heavily?

Well, without anything else to hold onto this game isn't really good.
A  good solid story could have elevated this to something memorable.
And I'm not even saying that they had to tell me everything, but they needed to get me engaged. A story that encapsulates the main character's attempts as survival would have been fine.
But the main character barely speaks, has no character to speak of. You can save around four to five people, of which almost all will be dead by the end of the story with little impact. You won't know why you're going forward beyond "A woman told me to" and the end of the game really feels like a slap in the face with either of the endings not really showing any impact from your efforts.

Is it a bad game? No.
But it's not a good game either. It's long, and without a good story it's boring.

I could see this engine being used to make a better game.
But my suggestion is: If you want it? Wait for a sale.

I was super close not to recommend The Surge and give a review based on pure frustration and rage. If you always despised runbacks in the Dark Souls series, you will find a new level of hate here, and it's not even about the bosses.

In The Surge, you have one hub (acting like a bonfire) per every bigger area plus a lot of shortcuts that need to be found and unlocked first. As a result, you will find yourself roaming through the same corridors with a sh!tload of dead ends. There's a high chance you will die randomly after a 5-minute run to the door that unlocks a shortcut, completely forgetting the path you took to get there in the first place.

The runbacks and backtracking wouldn't be that bad if the scenography was a little more diverse. Instead, the only 'biome' in the game is an abandoned factory with thousands of the same-looking rooms, hallways, and passageways. Most of the time, it's hard to tell where you are until you finally become familiar with this maddening maze.

THAT SAID, I'm still having a blast with this game. The combat system is directly linked to crafting - you have to target particular limbs and cut them in order to unlock new schematics (for the armor part/weapon the enemy has) or gather upgrade materials. You can also choose to target the most vulnerable spots to kill an enemy faster or just fight without targeting at all.

There is also an implant system that lets you change your build on the fly (in one of the hubs) - while pretty interesting, I feel most of the players will stuff the majority of available implant slots with health buffs, at least at the beginning of the journey. However, it lets you play a lot with the combat strategy later on when you unlock all the available implant slots and find the most interesting implants in the game world.

All in all, it's a bit different take on Souls games but super enjoyable nevertheless. You can also get it very cheap on sale with all the DLCs included and it's  totally worth it - both 'The Good, the Bad and the Augmented' and 'A Walk in the Park' make a good break from the abandoned factory theme and let you enjoy the combat in different sceneries.

I'll start off with a few tidbits some people seem to think are relevant:
Out of the entire so-called "Soulborne" series, I've only played Dark Souls III and all its DLC, which I liked a lot.
I'm on NG+ in this game.
I am primarily a PvE player in all games I play.

This game is not like Dark Souls. It does not try to be, and it does not want to be. To even say that it borrows elements from Dark Souls because it's hard is like saying that Dark Souls borrows elements from World of Warcraft because they're both RPGs. However, because many people think of this as "another Souls clone", I will include comparisons to Dark Souls at the end of each pro.

Pros:

The Surge does a good job of storytelling, if you're paying attention. You can get a pretty clear picture of what's going on through audio logs, announcements, NPCs, watching some in-game propaganda videos, or, if you're feeling up to it, reading flavor text. However, the story is not given to you all at the same time, or even in a linear manner. You're going to have bits and pieces out of sequence that you need to put together, like a puzzle. This is different from most other games, but, again, if you're paying attention, you'll come to like it.
This is different from Dark Souls, in that storytelling comes primarily from cutscenes and tons of flavor text.

Level design is mostly realistic. You're stuck in a factory, so there are catwalks, deadly drops, heavy machinery, crates, elevators, and your weapons are just tools being used as weapons. Detailed maps can be found in some areas, but mostly you'll find arrows pointing you in one direction or another. If you're an immersive gamer, like me, you'll love it.
This is no different from Dark Souls, with the exception that non-boss enemies in The Surge can be primarily found in tight spaces, leaving less room for error.

The looting system is deterministic, which is great, and realistic. If you want an armor schematic, you need to cut off pieces of it from enemies who wear it.
If you want components to craft and upgrade your current armor, you need to cut off the same pieces from enemies. If you want leg upgrades, you have to cut off the legs of enemies wearing leg armor. If you want torso upgrades, same thing. Unlike trying to get schematics, you do not need to cut off parts from enemies wearing the same armor as you.
This is different from Dark Souls, in that drops are almost completely random, with few exceptions.

Combat is also realistic, to some degree. Staggering enemies is difficult with lighter weapons with high attack speeds, but at the same time, heavier weapons capable of staggering enemies are harder to hit due to their low attack speed. Furthermore, to get a successful cut, you'll need to weaken enemy body parts. You also can't just back off from an attack past a certain point, due to momentum. Blocking also takes a heavy toll on your stamina, and just holding the block will slowly deplete your stamina. You are, after all, using heavy machinery as weapons. You need to be careful about when to attack and which weapon to use against an enemy.
This is different from Dark Souls, where you can cancel just about any attack by rolling, eliminating the risk of going "all in", and shields simply slow stamina regeneration..

The implant and armor systems are realistic. Your implants need power, but your RIG also needs power to help you move around, so heavy armor will leave you unable to use many implants, while implants will force you to use light armor. That is, unless you farm scrap and level up until you can have both. However, armor still has drawbacks. Heavy armor typically increases stamina and energy consumption and may even decrease damage output.
This is different from Dark Souls, where you need to meet attribute requirements to effectively use weapons and armor, yet suffer no penalties as long as your load capacity is high enough, unless otherwise specified by your weapons and armor.

Cons:

Storytelling has some flaws, primarily in the form of NPCs. Every NPC you talk to says they don't know what's going on, which gets tedious after a while. Although it is realistic, given the situation, it's also frustrating for players due to the inclusion of a "What's going on here?" dialogue option with every single NPC you meet.

Level design can be confusing. Although the developers had the right idea by limiting the amount of maps and such, there's a lack of signs that is unrealistic in a large manufacturing complex where people are expected to move around on foot.

Combat can be frustrating at first in NG+. In NG, you start with what amounts to Mk 0 armor and weapons, and enemies (damage, HP, armor) are scaled to that. Throughout NG, you can upgrade your weapons and armor all the way to Mk V by finding upgrade items called "nano cores". However, there's a limited number of these, so you'll most likely just upgrade your armor and weapons to Mk IV. In NG+, however, the "baseline" from which enemies in the first area are scaled is now Mk VI, meaning that your Mk IV armor and weapons are effectively worse by comparison than your "Mk 0" armor and weapons from NG. This can lead to some quick, frustrating deaths in the early levels, until you upgrade everything to Mk VI.

Upgrading can also be frustrating in NG+. Because you can't farm Mk I - Mk IV components any more, you jump straight to Mk VI. However, this also incurs a massive increase in scrap costs, since you're effectively upgrading multiple times all at once. If you plan on using multiple weapons in NG+, but didn't previously upgrade them, you may spend a lot of time farming.



All in all, this is a good game, well worth the money. Just don't think it's Dark Souls, because it's not.

The Surge is a souls-like game that really impressed me. The story is lackluster, but the gameplay is simply put, amazing.

The combat in this game is so dynamic and fluid. Each weapon type (and sometimes weapon itself) has its own really cool, flashy set of combos for you to learn and experiment with, to find what works best.  You're not locked into any spec or anything like that, you just do what you want.

I'm bad at writing these, but I had to write something, because I truly loved this game.

I like to think I am an even-tempered man. I don't honk at the guy in front of me when I'm stuck in traffic, and I grumble only mildly at inclement weather. 

With that in mind, this game has made me rage-quit only to start it back up hours later multiple times. You will want to tear your hair out with frustration, but you will keep coming back for more. And I mean that in the best possible sense.

I tend to write really long rambling reviews, so I am giving the short version up front. The Surge is a sci-fi game clearly inspired by the Dark Souls series, but it does enough twists to the formula that I think it deserves to be seen as its own thing, not just a copy. Some of those twists work well and others fall flat. It took me ~35 hours to beat the main story and one of the two DLCs. There is some jank and the game crashed a couple times. Overall I had fun playing The Surge, but I was ready to stop playing after that point and didn’t feel the need to do the second DLC. If you like Souls games and want to try something weird and experimental then this is highly recommended.

That’s the short version, here’s the long version:

Controls: Your character is a guy who volunteered to get bolted into an exo-skeleton because an accident left him partially paralyzed. The procedure did not go well and now everything is going crazy. The game does a very good job of making you feel like you’re riding around in a metal frame. Jump distances are long, fall damage is super generous (you can die to fall damage, but it takes a LONG drop), and there is no such thing as carry capacity/fat rolling. The downside is that your movement feels a little stiff and you don’t always have a ton of fine control of where you’re moving. That normally doesn’t matter, but there’s a couple platforming parts where it is noticeable. 

Combat: The combat is very original. The controls don’t feel like a normal Souls game. It reminds me a lot more of a weapon based fighting game like For Honor with lots of elaborate combos. It is an interesting way to play, but I am not sure the depth of the combat system is really necessary. I found myself ignoring most of it. The reason for all this complexity is that the game tries to make every enemy feel threatening and challenging. You will usually only be fighting 1-2 enemies at once and those enemies can very easily ruin your day if you get unlucky or make a mistake.

You use the right stick to lock onto various body parts of your target. Attacks will do more damage to an unarmored part, and if you do enough damage to a certain body part you can do a finisher where you cut it off and get whatever armor or weapons were on that part (or melt them into upgrade materials if you already have them). This system works pretty well, but unless you are grinding for specific things you will most likely just target whatever part of the enemy is unarmored. The system really shines in the small roster of bosses. They’re all unique and you actively knock parts off them as you fight based on where you hit them. That can change their moves and behavior. Kind of like Monster Hunter, but even moreso. 

The standard enemy roster is really cool. I just wish the weird enemies showed up more since 75% of what you fight is “generic human in exo-skeleton”. The developers really tried to be creative here. There are enemies that stand back up after you cut a piece off them, enemies that have medkits on their back you can sneak up to and heal, enemies that change where their armor is based on where you’re hitting them, and several other gimmicks. Most of these work really well and there are also some non-humanoid drones or larger security robots that show up and provide variety.

Gear: The weapon roster makes me feel like a kid in a candy store. Picture every power tool you can think of: drills, circular saws, impact hammers, plasma cutters, arc welders, etc. Now imagine one of those bolted to your arm! You can even smack people with the business end of a forklift. I get the feeling the game pushes you towards smaller faster weapons, but I completed it just fine with a bigger one. There are no ranged weapons or magic equivalent, but you do have a drone that you can activate to shoot a little laser or do other utility type stuff. I found it pretty pointless, but YMMV. 

Armor has a really cool system where each part will give your character not just protection and poise, but also stat modifiers (attack speed/impact, damage modifiers to armored/unarmored parts, stamina consumption modifiers, etc). Armor also has set bonuses which can be very powerful, so you most likely will not be mixing and matching. There are damage types in the game, but they aren’t explained very well and rarely matter very much.

Leveling up: So far everything has ranged from “really cool” to “interesting idea that worked ok”. I think leveling up is where this game goes off the rails. They tried for versatility and simplicity, but they missed the mark in my opinion. There are no stats to put points in. When you accumulate enough scrap (souls) to level up you just raise one number called “core power”. Each armor piece costs a certain amount of power to equip. Heavier armor usually costs more power, but also comes with downsides like slower attack speed or more stamina consumption, so you kind of get double penalized for being a tank. 

You also have implant slots and implants cost power to equip. Think of these like rings in a Souls game, except you get a lot of slots and most of them can only get swapped at a bonfire. Implants basically do everything in this game. Want more health? Implant. Want an estus? Implant (multiple implants if you want more charges). Heck, want to see the enemy health bars? Implant. The slots fill up fast, especially early game when you don’t have as many, and you often go back and forth between “not enough slots to hold everything you want” and “not enough power to fill all your slots”. It also can be rough early game because you can never have more health/stamina unless you find more implants that boost those stats. In general it makes leveling up feel unrewarding. You do get more powerful and at some point around 2/3 through the game the switch clicks and you become an unstoppable engine of destruction, but you don’t necessarily feel like you’re getting stronger until you reach that point.

World/theme: I love when a game that is traditionally fantasy gets a sci-fi treatment. This is a harder near future take on sci-fi. Imagine running through a SpaceX launch facility using repurposed industrial tools to smack people who turned into zombies when an EMP shorted out all their neural link implants. If that sentence does it for you then you’ll love this game. The story is generally pretty good. I tend not to like “big corporation bad” stories, but this one has enough depth that I’m ok with it. There’s multiple factions working inside this company to try and accomplish different things, sometimes not even aware of each other, so it feels a lot more like a collection of people and not some faceless monolith that only exists because they need a bad guy.

The level design is pretty cool. There’s one bonfire per area and a ton of circular paths that go out from it. The standard loop is “pick a path, do some exploring, fight some enemies, get a reward/unlock another path, unlock a shortcut back to the bonfire”. The shortcuts and areas all fit together really well and don’t feel too much like a maze, although if you set the game down for a while then come back to it you will get hopelessly lost until you remember where things are. Different areas have different themes and the game does a great job of not always looking the same. There are minimal death pits, but there are a couple areas where you question why the developers put enemies there, because you really don’t want to be fighting. Since every enemy is a threat it tends to make for lots of twisty corridors or cluttered areas to break up line of sight (which also comes with the “turn around a blind corner and immediately get ambushed” problem). Enemies have long patrol paths and are surprisingly alert. They will totally come in like a freight train to ruin your day from across the map if they get line of sight to you. You almost have to play it like a stealth game in a couple areas.

Playing through the Surge has been one of the most enjoyable gaming experiences I have had to date. Everyone knows it's a souls like game but it is much more than that at heart.

It's easy to brush off the story at play here but I urge everyone to actually pay attention. Listen to the audiologs. Explore everything. Do the side quests. It's hard for a game like this - not focused on story but focused around it's difficulty and core gameplay loops to engage you in a thought out story, and while I admit it wasn't the best told tale it was certainly an interesting one. There are plenty of seemingly pointless audio logs or focus points that will all be revealed later on in the game and all of them will open your eyes to how grim the world of the Surge really is. Had it been a little more polished and perhaps given some background lore this would have been one of the best stories in gaming, in my opinion.

Aside from my love of the story, the game has many selling points.

- The combat is very, very satisfying. Yes it recycles the core dark souls style but it adds to it and IMO improves on it. With execution moves and pinpoint targeting you really feel in control in the fights you get into. The actual difficulty in fighting enemies I feel was greater than any other souls like game I have played (DS1,2 and 3) and I initially it a serious wall in combat. Practice truly does make perfect though and the game will reward you for trying again, because once you get the hang of your preferred weapon (of which there are tonnes) and can learn off some enemy move sets you'll be making your way through enemies like greased lighting.

-Customization is also plentiful. The Surge doesn't let you sink EXP points into any given skills or any of those familiar rpg mechanics you may be used to, but instead it has its very unique implant system. These implants allow you to drastically change up your playstyle and as you progress further into the game and find more you can adapt and overcome most situations. All of these implants rely on your core power which is in essence the exp sink of the game, but it doesn't increase your base stats, and will only allow you to add more implants or equip more powerful gear. It was an odd system to me when I first started but I like what they have done. I can choose to go into a fight stacked with HP implants and healing implants, or I can throw caution to the wind and only take DPS implants. High risk high reward gameplay is ever present in the Surge and the implant system simply puts the cherry on top.

-The game is gorgeous. Now I realize it is set indoors in familiar environments like 80% of the time but my god are those environments well done. The textures are beautiful and everything looks perfect. There are some sections when you walk through tunnels and I personally had to stop and admire my character model during some of these instances when the light hit me a certain way. It's easy to say that everything in the game looks the same because they're all robots and everything is mechanical etc. But looking similar doesn't mean looking bad.

-There are plenty of nifty little things that make the game so much more enjoyable. Set bonuses, secret areas, collectibles, easter eggs, ironic humour and more. 


There is an abundance of things to do in the NG mode and then plenty of farming and upgrades and extra goodies in NG+, there is a DLC that just came out too so you won't be stuck for content in the slightest. Any souls fan is missing out big time if they pass up on this game, even if the setting doesn't appeal to you I urge you to try it because it will grow on you and you will love it.

The game has some quirks but when you get used to them (or learn to ignore some of them outright) it becomes an interesting sci-fi souls-like that is more similar to Dark Souls 1 than to modern entries.

You have only one "bonefire" per area which sounds weird at first because navigating the levels with only one checkpoint seems like a chore and you might think that you will have to traverse the same rooms again and again. But the game compensates for it with a lot of shortcuts. On the one hand those shortcuts do the job; but on the other hand this system with one checkpoint and many shortcuts turns the areas into mazes. Sometimes those shortcuts are just a bunch of service tunnels that sprawl though the level, which feels like a lazy design choice that had to be done because of this self-imposed limitation. Some shortcuts are smarter and tie nicely together like a locked door to a previous section or a lift. But most of them are just service tunnels, especially in the second half of the game.

Combat is focused on hit-and-run - dodge, wait for an enemy to finish their combo, hitting them after that, repeat. The limb targeting ties in nicely with that process. The main point is figuring out your weapon - when to hit, how many times to hit and when to fall back. Weapons variety is good so if one doesn't work for you you can always try another.
Blocking feels useful only for countering. If you try to block every attack you will run out of stamina very quickly.
You can also jump and duck while dodging but I almost never found it useful apart from fighting one specific enemy. It seems like this mechanic was developed specifically for this enemy.

The quirks with the combat:
1) wonky hitboxes - sometimes you get hit when you think you are clear which can cost you a lot of HP (see next point);

Seven years after I first played the demo for The Surge, I've finally completed it.  My thanks to WheatStoneHolmes for giving me a copy of the full game way back in 2019.

I feel like gamers didn't appreciate this game enough.  Recently I've seen so many AAA games with much larger budgets, development teams, and gameplay features still only amount to “zog-slop” gamer gruel; totally soulless gaming experiences that struggle to make the player feel [i]anything[/i] at any point in their bloated 60+ hr. runtimes.

The Surge was a mid-2010s AA game that has a strong current of inspiration running through it.  It keeps things simple and focused.

The theme is the inevitable self-destruction that will result from mankind's relentless pursuit of technological development.  Even the new technological "solutions" to the earlier problems, themselves caused caused by earlier technological "solutions," cause new problems, in an infinite progression of futility.  A character encountered in The Surge is perceptive enough to see this futile cycle and he uses technology to develop a process to end it, once and for all.  99.8% fatalities are predicted.

The developers were able to carry this technological theme over to the gameplay.  Rather than the player character having inherent stats that increase as he levels up like 99% of RPGs, in The Surge ALL stats are tied to external equipment and implants.  In keeping with modern approaches to applying technology, everything is modular and replacable at the player's will.  No character development decisions are ever permanent.

The Surge is a very thoughtfully-made game.  There's no point in me reviewing game mechanics so long after its release.  It was fun and challenging, but what's really gonna stick with me is how it showed humanity pushed to the brink by a mindless commitment to technological development, efficiency and problem-solving.  It's getting at a real, deeper aspect of the modern era that often goes unnoticed and uncriticized.

I bought The Surge 2 and when I play it (someday!), I hope for more exploration of these themes.  They're perfect for an ultra-dark setting and morbid storytelling.

I had a lot of fun playing this game. Not the first sentence you'd expect from a negative review, but it's true. The thing is, I've also had a lot of frustration and annoyance, and I'm fairly certain the amount of times I've said "F*** THIS GAME" is much higher than the number of moments of joy and satisfaction.
So, seeing as Steam has no "meh" button, I've decided to go with negative.

Now, why did I find this so frustrating and annoying? You're probably guessing it's because the game is hard - Dark Souls-like combat with bosses that require endless attempts to defeat and serious punishment for death. Well, no. That wasn't it. It was pretty much everything else.

First - a disclaimer: I haven't played Dark Souls. Don't know if I'd like it. But from what I've seen, it looks like Dark Souls can get away with a lot of the things it does, while this game can't.
First off, no minimap. In Dark Souls, the environments are different, each area has it's own unique design, sometimes you're out in the open sky and can see the view, tell where you're headed, and remember the layout. In The Surge though, everything looks the same. You spend half the game in tunnels that look exactly the same, fighting enemies that look exactly the same, and the level layouts get more and more confusing as the game progresses. It gets so bad that even if you give up and go online looking for an explanation on how to get where you need to be, you'll find threads where people genuinely struggle to give instructions because everything just looks exactly the same.

Next up we have the story. To be perfectly honest, even after finishing the game, I'm not 100% sure what the story was, or why things happened the way they did. I didn't care about any of the characters, and even the moments that were supposed to spark some emotion fell very flat. So that's not something you're going to find here.

The combat was pretty fun. It's your regular stamina-based combat with blocking and dodging (though honestly I gave up on blocking very early on as it takes up more stamina and isn't very useful. Dodging alone is 100% enough to beat the game), but there's a bit of a twist. To upgrade you gear, you gotta chop armor/weapon parts off of enemies, which means targeting their armored limbs rather than the unarmored one. That forces you to choose - make the combat harder by attacking armored parts, removing knockback and doing less damage, or make it easier on yourself and attack their bare bits but get no materials. It's an interesting mechanic that is used quite well, and is the main thing the game has going for it imo.
Boss fights weren't very interesting to me. Maybe I was expecting too much, seeing as this is a Souls-like and I've heard so much about how hard the bosses in Dark Souls are, but whether that's true for dark souls or not, it's not true for this game. Bosses aren't very hard, they just have a "catch". Maybe you gotta run between their legs while they're shooting you, maybe you gotta attack only after a specific attack, maybe you gotta trick them into shooting a part of the environment, etc. After a few tries, with the incredible power of trial and error, you'll figure it out, and that's that. Boss fights don't require you to be quick or precise, just patient. As a result, while they do take several tries, the victory isn't actually all that satisfying. Compared to, for example, Hollow Knight (which I really enjoyed), that required genuine skill, speed and precision, this type of boss fight is pretty lame.

And last but not least, there's just some stupid annoying crap all over the game design. For example, when you die fighting the final boss, you respawn facing the exit of the area. Naturally, your first instinct is to immediately run forward after respawning to get back in the fight - Which moves you OUT of the area and into a loading screen which you have to wait through before turning around and waiting through another loading screen. God that was annoying. Another annoying thing is that, at the end game, you get blueprints for better weapons and armor, but to craft them you need Mk.1 materials which you can only get at the starter area. So you literally have to run ALL the way back to the start if you want to craft them. WTF. I guess they're just given to you so you can build them during NG+ or something, but f*** that.

So yeah, that's that. As you can see, I enjoyed parts of it, I stuck around till the end (even though I genuinely had to force myself to get through the final section), but overall, I can't recommend it. There are so many Dark Souls clones out there that even if that's your thing, you're probably better off playing a different one.
